domains.name: Critical & Multiple-Text Reading
domains.summary: This domain addresses reading as evaluation and integration: reconstructing arguments, evaluating evidence and methods, surfacing assumptions and perspective, reading theoretical texts, reading across multiple sources and mapping literatures, and moving from comprehension to a reasoned response that serves writing. Critical reading is presented as questioning and evaluating rather than fault-finding, and as partly discipline-specific; the notion of critical thinking is itself contested in EAP. Research on multiple-document reading shows that attending to sources and integrating across texts are distinct skills that do not develop automatically from single-text comprehension.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to identify and judge the arguments and evidence in what you read, notice assumptions and perspectives, compare and connect several sources, map a body of research, and form your own reasoned response for discussion and writing.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce critical reading through accessible argumentative texts, focusing on argument identification, critical questions and short reasoned responses.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Link critical reading to source-based writing: identifying arguments, evaluating evidence, reading for an assignment and responding critically to sources.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply critical reading to disciplinary sources, including multiple texts and empirical studies, with attention to assumptions and perspective.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise methods critique, multiple-text integration and literature mapping for assignments and the dissertation.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on mapping and positioning within a literature, reading theoretical texts and critiquing methods at a specialist level.

domains.name: Reading Processes & Fluency
domains.summary: This domain covers the cognitive and linguistic foundations of academic reading: automatic word recognition, parsing of compressed academic sentences, reading fluency and volume, and the way these lower-level processes interact with background knowledge, purpose and reading load. L2 reading research finds that L2 vocabulary and grammatical knowledge are the strongest correlates of L2 reading comprehension, so the domain prioritises building the linguistic base and reading volume on which strategies depend rather than treating strategies as a substitute for them. It also addresses the practical conditions of university reading: on-screen texts, long reading lists and the legitimate, checked use of a reader's other languages.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how reading works, why knowing more words and reading more makes everything else easier, and how to read more fluently, cope with long reading lists, read well on screen and use your other languages wisely.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build automaticity and reading volume through extensive reading of graded and accessible texts, alongside explicit work on parsing long sentences, background knowledge and reading purpose.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Diagnose each learner's vocabulary size and reading rate early, set realistic fluency targets, and introduce reading-load management and on-screen reading of authentic disciplinary texts.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Focus on coping with module reading lists, dense textbook and article prose, and strategic, transparent use of L1 resources and machine translation.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise triage of large reading loads on compressed timelines, deliberate background-knowledge building for students changing discipline, and efficient on-screen reading.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address sustainable reading of large literatures, realistic rate expectations for specialist and theoretical texts, and the place of plurilingual reading in research.

domains.name: Reading Strategies & Comprehension
domains.summary: This domain covers the strategies and comprehension skills that turn decoded text into usable understanding: previewing, selective reading, identifying main ideas and text organisation, tracking reference and stance, inferring, monitoring and repairing comprehension, annotating, and integrating prose with visuals. Strategy instruction has positive but variable average effects, and its benefits depend on learners having enough language knowledge to apply strategies to the text at hand. Skimming and scanning are often over-represented in materials shaped by test formats relative to the careful reading for learning and argument that dominates university study, so the domain gives priority to main ideas, structure, reference and stance, and treats speeded strategies as tools for specific purposes.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to get an overview of a text, find and follow its main ideas and structure, work out what is implied and whose view is being expressed, notice when you have lost understanding and fix it, and read graphs and tables together with the text.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Prioritise paragraph and text structure, main ideas, reference tracking and textbook reading, with strategies modelled on accessible texts.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Integrate strategies with careful reading of authentic academic texts used in source-based assignments, and avoid test-driven over-emphasis on skimming and scanning.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply strategies to disciplinary textbooks and early encounters with research articles, with emphasis on stance, inference and visuals.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on research-article navigation, stance and efficient previewing of large numbers of sources.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address fine-grained stance reading, comprehension monitoring with specialist texts and efficient navigation of research literature.

topics.name: What critical reading involves
topics.description: Understand critical reading as actively questioning a text's purpose, claims, evidence, reasoning, assumptions and significance in order to judge its value for one's own purposes, which includes recognising strengths as well as weaknesses. What counts as critical varies across disciplines, and the concept of critical thinking is itself contested, so learners need to see critical reading modelled in their field rather than as a universal checklist or as fault-finding.
masteryEvidence: Explains, with an example, the difference between describing what a text says and evaluating it
Identifies both a strength and a limitation of a text and justifies each
Checks the accuracy of their own reading before critiquing a text
Describes what critical reading involves in their own discipline, for example evaluating methods, interpretations or theoretical framing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to read a short argumentative article and say what makes it convincing and what makes it less convincing. Check whether they evaluate with reasons rather than summarise, whether they acknowledge strengths, and whether their critique rests on an accurate reading of the text.

topics.name: Identifying arguments in texts
topics.description: Locate and reconstruct a writer's argument by identifying the main claim, the reasons and evidence offered, intermediate conclusions and the counter-arguments addressed, distinguishing argument from description, explanation and background. Reconstructing an argument accurately is the precondition for evaluating it and for representing it fairly in one's own writing.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the main claim of a text and the sentence or sentences that state it
Lists the reasons and evidence offered and links each to the claim it supports
Distinguishes argumentative passages from descriptive or explanatory ones
Reconstructs the argument as an outline or map that the writer would recognise as fair
Identifies the counter-arguments the writer addresses and how each is handled
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 500-word argumentative text and ask the learner for a claim–reasons–evidence outline. Check whether the main claim is a contestable statement rather than a topic, whether reasons are distinguished from evidence, and whether background material is excluded.

topics.name: Evaluating evidence in texts
topics.description: Judge whether the evidence a text offers is relevant to its claims, sufficient for their scope and of adequate quality, taking into account the type of evidence (empirical data, statistics, expert opinion, cases, anecdote), its provenance and whether the reasoning from evidence to claim is sound. Evaluating evidence determines how far a source can be relied on and how it should be represented.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the type of evidence offered for each main claim
Judges whether evidence is relevant and sufficient for the scope of the claim, for example a single case offered for a general claim
Recognises common weaknesses such as anecdote presented as general evidence, correlation presented as causation and outdated data
Distinguishes the quality of evidence from how persuasively it is presented
Formulates a calibrated judgement of how strongly the evidence supports the claim
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short text that makes a general claim supported by one survey statistic and one anecdote, and ask how well the claim is supported. Strong responses note the mismatch between the scope of the claim and the evidence and the limits of each evidence type; weak responses accept the claim, or dismiss it, without specific reasons.

topics.name: Identifying assumptions and values
topics.description: Surface the unstated premises, values and framings on which an argument depends, including the assumptions that link evidence to claims, assumptions about definitions and scope, and value assumptions about what matters. Assumptions are often where disagreement between texts and disciplines really lies, and identifying them allows fair rather than superficial critique.
masteryEvidence: States an unstated premise that an argument needs in order to work
Identifies the warrant linking a given piece of evidence to a claim
Recognises value assumptions in a framing, such as prioritising efficiency over equity
Explains how a different assumption would change the conclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short argument with an implicit premise, such as a policy recommendation drawn from economic data, and ask what must be assumed for the conclusion to follow. Check whether the learner states a genuine missing premise rather than restating the claim or raising an unrelated objection.

topics.name: Recognising bias and perspective
topics.description: Recognise how a text's perspective is shaped by its author's position, interests, funding, disciplinary or theoretical commitments and intended audience, and how this shows in the selection of evidence, framing and language. Recognising perspective is not the same as dismissing a text as biased: all texts are written from a position, so readers judge how that position affects reliability and which perspectives are missing, while also attending to their own biases as readers.
masteryEvidence: Identifies an author's position, affiliation or interests and explains how they might shape the text
Points to framing choices (terminology, metaphor, what is foregrounded) that reflect a perspective
Identifies relevant evidence or perspectives that a text omits
Distinguishes a legitimate perspective from distortion or misrepresentation of evidence
Reflects on how their own prior views affect their evaluation of a text
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give two short texts on the same issue from organisations with different interests, such as an industry body and a campaigning group. Ask how each frames the issue, what evidence each selects and what each omits. Check whether the learner identifies concrete framing and selection features rather than simply labelling one text 'biased'.

topics.name: Reading methods critically
topics.description: Evaluate the design of empirical studies at the level of an informed non-specialist: whether the sample and setting support the generalisations made, whether measures capture the construct, whether the design supports causal claims, how data were analysed and whether limitations are acknowledged. Criteria differ between quantitative and qualitative research and across disciplines; formal discipline-specific appraisal tools belong to dhl.critical-appraisal and to methods training.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the design, sample or data, measures and analysis of a study from its methods section
Judges whether the sample and setting support the scope of the conclusions
Recognises when a design cannot support a causal claim
Distinguishes statistical significance from practical importance at a basic level
Identifies limitations the authors acknowledge and at least one they do not
Applies criteria suited to qualitative research, such as transparency of analysis and richness of data, instead of judging it by quantitative criteria
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the abstract and methods section of a small study whose conclusion over-generalises, for example a single-site convenience sample used to support a national claim. Ask whether the conclusion is justified. Check whether the learner connects specific design features to the scope of the claim rather than offering generic criticisms such as 'the sample is small'.

topics.name: Reading across multiple texts
topics.description: Read across several texts on a topic by attending to source information (who wrote it, when, where and for whom), identifying where texts agree, conflict or address different questions, corroborating claims, and building an integrated understanding that keeps track of which source said what. Multiple-text comprehension is distinct from single-text comprehension and is the reading basis of synthesis in writing.
masteryEvidence: Records source information for each text and uses it when weighing conflicting claims
Identifies points of agreement, disagreement and complementarity across texts
Explains plausible reasons for disagreement, such as different methods, contexts, definitions or interests
Constructs an integrated account of an issue that attributes each point to its source or sources
Corroborates a claim against other sources before relying on it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three short texts that partly conflict on an issue and ask for a brief account of what is known, indicating where the sources agree and disagree and why they might differ. Check source attribution, identification of conflicts and the plausibility of the explanations offered.

topics.name: Reading for a writing task
topics.description: Select, read and organise sources around a specific writing task: analysing the question to set reading priorities, reading for what the task needs, noting material in usable form with full source details, and reading with the developing argument in mind. Most university writing is source-based, and both the efficiency and the integrity of source use depend on how the reading was done.
masteryEvidence: Derives reading priorities and search directions from the assignment question
Selects sources and sections relevant to the question and justifies the choices
Organises notes by the points the task requires rather than by source alone
Records bibliographic details and distinguishes quotation, paraphrase and own comment in notes
Revises reading priorities as the argument develops
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an essay question and five sources of varying relevance. Ask the learner which they would use, which sections they would read and how they would organise their notes. Check that choices follow from the question and that the note plan supports an argument rather than summarising each source in turn.

topics.name: Mapping a body of literature
topics.description: Map a body of literature by identifying its main themes, debates, methodological approaches, key authors and schools of thought, and how they relate to one another over time, so that one's own work can be positioned within the scholarly conversation. Mapping is iterative and moves the reader from accumulating sources to understanding the structure of a field.
masteryEvidence: Produces a map or matrix of a literature showing themes, positions and key contributors
Identifies the main debates in a field and the positions taken within them
Recognises influential works and how later work builds on or challenges them
Identifies methodological trends and under-researched areas
Explains where their own question sits within the map
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to bring ten sources they have read on their topic and draw a map grouping them by theme or position, with lines showing relationships. Check whether groupings are conceptual rather than by date or source type, and whether debates and gaps are visible on the map.

topics.name: Reading theoretical and conceptual texts
topics.description: Read dense theoretical and conceptual texts, common in the humanities and social sciences, by identifying key concepts and how the author defines them, reconstructing the argument at the level of ideas, relating abstractions to examples, and situating the text within the debate it addresses. Theoretical prose combines high abstraction, nominalisation and specialised senses of everyday words, and usually requires more than one reading.
masteryEvidence: Identifies and defines the key concepts of a theoretical text in the author's own terms
Reconstructs the central argument in plain language
Relates abstract claims to concrete examples, including examples of their own
Identifies the position the text argues against or builds on
Recognises when a term is used in a theory-specific sense different from everyday usage
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 600–800-word theoretical extract. Ask the learner to define its two key concepts as the author uses them, restate the main argument in three sentences and give one example of their own that illustrates it. Check fidelity to the author's definitions and whether the example genuinely fits.

topics.name: Generating critical questions
topics.description: Generate and apply a set of critical questions to interrogate a text systematically: its purpose and audience, its main claims, the evidence and reasoning behind them, its assumptions and perspective, what it omits, and its implications and usefulness for the reader's purpose. Question sets are scaffolds to be internalised and adapted to disciplinary norms, not checklists to be completed mechanically.
masteryEvidence: Applies a question set to a text and gives answers grounded in the text
Generates questions specific to the text and discipline rather than only generic ones
Prioritises the questions most relevant to their reading purpose
Uses critical questions to prepare seminar contributions or plan a critique
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short text and ask the learner to write five questions they would ask of it, then answer two. Check whether the questions go beyond comprehension to address claims, evidence, assumptions and implications, and whether the answers are grounded in the text.

topics.name: Formulating a critical response
topics.description: Move from comprehension and analysis to a reasoned evaluation of a text: state a position on its claims, value or usefulness, support it with reasons and evidence from analysis of the text and other sources, and express it with appropriate qualification. A critical response is neither a summary nor an unsupported opinion but an argued judgement that can be defended in discussion or writing.
masteryEvidence: States a clear, appropriately qualified evaluative position on a text
Supports the position with reasons linked to specific features of the text's argument or evidence
Acknowledges strengths as well as limitations
Relates the text to other sources or contexts where relevant
Keeps the author's views and their own clearly distinct in speech and writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write a 150-word response to a short argumentative article. Check whether it contains a position, reasons linked to specific features of the text, acknowledgement of both strengths and limitations, and a clear separation between the author's views and the learner's.

topics.name: Reading as an interactive process
topics.description: Understand comprehension as the interaction of lower-level processes (word recognition, syntactic parsing, forming propositions) with higher-level processes (building a model of what the text says and integrating it with background knowledge, purpose and inference). The concept explains why L2 readers who know many strategies can still fail when lexical and grammatical processing is slow or inaccurate, and gives learners and teachers a shared vocabulary for diagnosing reading problems.
masteryEvidence: Explains, using an example from their own reading, how an unknown word or a misparsed sentence caused a comprehension failure that background knowledge could not repair
Distinguishes between what a text states and the interpretation they built from it when discussing a passage
Classifies a given comprehension difficulty as mainly lexical, grammatical, discourse-level or knowledge-related
Proposes a remedy matched to each type of difficulty (vocabulary work, sentence analysis, building topic knowledge) rather than defaulting to a generic strategy
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 150-word academic paragraph on an unfamiliar topic and ask them to mark where they lost understanding and say why. Check whether they attribute breakdowns to specific causes (an unknown word, a long subject noun phrase, missing topic knowledge) rather than reporting only that the text was difficult.

topics.name: Automatic word recognition
topics.description: Recognise frequent and core academic words quickly and accurately enough that recognition demands little attention, freeing working memory for building meaning. Recognition speed depends on the quality of stored form–meaning knowledge and is shaped by the reader's first-language writing system, so it develops mainly through large amounts of reading and timed practice with known words rather than through strategy instruction.
masteryEvidence: Recognises high-frequency and core academic words in context with near-ceiling accuracy and without visible decoding effort
Recognises inflected and derived forms of known words (analyse, analysed, analysis, analytical) as members of one family on sight
Distinguishes visually similar academic words (adapt/adopt, casual/causal, affect/effect) without marked slowing
Shows increasing speed across a course on timed recognition or sentence-verification tasks built from known vocabulary
topics.assessmentPrompt: Run a two-minute timed task of 40 short sentences built from high-frequency and core academic vocabulary, each to be judged sensible or nonsensical. Compare accuracy and items completed with the cohort: a learner who is accurate but very slow needs fluency practice, whereas one who is inaccurate on common words needs vocabulary-base work.

topics.name: Reading fluency and rate
topics.description: Read connected academic text at a rate appropriate to purpose while maintaining comprehension, and build that rate through timed reading of easy texts, repeated reading and extensive reading. Learners also develop realistic expectations: silent reading of expository text by skilled adult L1 readers averages roughly 200–300 words per minute, slower for dense or unfamiliar material, and claims that speed-reading techniques multiply rate without loss of comprehension are not supported by eye-movement and comprehension research.
masteryEvidence: Records reading rate and comprehension on timed passages and tracks both over a course
Increases rate on easy, lexically familiar texts across a programme while keeping comprehension stable
Varies rate deliberately according to text difficulty and purpose, slowing for dense argument and speeding up on familiar material
Explains why techniques promising very high rates, such as suppressing inner speech or taking in whole lines at a glance, trade comprehension for speed
Sets a personal rate target and practice plan grounded in their own measured baseline
topics.assessmentPrompt: Time the learner reading a 500-word text pitched well within their vocabulary level, then ask five comprehension questions without looking back. Calculate words per minute and the comprehension score. A fast reader with weak comprehension is skimming rather than reading; a slow reader with strong comprehension on easy text is a candidate for fluency practice; slow and weak suggests vocabulary or word-recognition gaps.

topics.name: Extensive reading
topics.description: Read large quantities of self-selected, linguistically easy material, such as graded readers, accessible non-fiction and popular science, for meaning and enjoyment, with minimal dictionary use and no intensive exercises attached. Extensive reading supports reading rate, consolidation and incidental growth of vocabulary, and confidence, but its gains accumulate over months, so it must be planned into a programme and continued beyond it rather than recommended in passing.
masteryEvidence: Selects texts at a level where nearly all running words are known, using a quick page check for unknown words
Maintains a reading log showing regular, sustained reading volume over several weeks
Abandons texts that prove too hard or uninteresting and chooses alternatives without treating this as failure
Progresses from graded readers towards accessible authentic texts in or near their intended field
Reports or demonstrates increased reading rate or ease over time
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to bring the text they are currently reading for extensive reading and to summarise the last few pages, noting any unknown words on one page. If they meet more than a few unknown words per page or cannot summarise easily, the text is too hard to function as extensive reading; help them choose a lower level.

topics.name: Reading with a purpose
topics.description: Set an explicit purpose before reading (to locate information, grasp gist, learn content, follow an argument, extract a method, integrate sources, write or evaluate) and adjust speed, depth, sequence and note-making to that purpose. Purpose-setting is what makes selective reading principled rather than careless, and it sets the standard for what counts as having understood a text well enough.
masteryEvidence: States before reading what they need from a text and how they will know when they have it
Chooses a reading approach that matches the stated purpose, for example careful linear reading of an argument to be critiqued but selective reading of a methods section to answer a design question
Changes approach mid-text when the text proves more or less relevant than expected
Explains, with reference to the task, why one text was read closely and another only in part
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner one article with two different tasks (for example, 'find the sample size' and 'decide whether the conclusion is justified') and ask them to describe how they will read for each before starting. Look for clearly different plans in scope, sequence, speed and notes, not 'read it all carefully' for both.

topics.name: Parsing complex academic sentences
topics.description: Analyse long academic sentences by locating the finite verb of the main clause, its subject and the head nouns of heavily modified noun phrases, so that the core proposition can be separated from embedded and qualifying material. Academic prose packs information into phrases (nominalisations, prepositional chains, pre- and post-modification) rather than clauses, so readers who parse as they would conversation often misidentify what a sentence claims.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the main-clause subject and finite verb in sentences of 35 words or more containing several embedded phrases
Locates the head noun of a long noun phrase and states what its pre- and post-modifiers add
Unpacks a nominalisation into a clause showing who did what (the reduction in emissions → emissions were reduced, by someone, for some reason)
Reduces a complex sentence to a short core statement that preserves its claim and its qualification
Detects when a misparse, such as reading a reduced relative participle as the main verb, has produced a reading that conflicts with the surrounding text
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three 30–50-word sentences from a textbook or article in their field. Ask them to bracket the subject, underline the main verb and write a core version of six to ten words for each. Check that the core preserves the actual claim rather than a noun taken from inside a modifying phrase.

topics.name: Background knowledge and schemata
topics.description: Recognise that comprehension depends on topic, disciplinary and text-type knowledge as well as language, and deliberately activate and build that knowledge before and during reading through accessible overviews, glossaries, textbooks and lectures. This explains why the same reader can read fluently in a familiar field yet struggle in a new one, and why building knowledge is a legitimate reading strategy, especially for postgraduates changing discipline.
masteryEvidence: Lists what they already know and expect about a topic before reading and revises the list afterwards
Uses an accessible source (textbook chapter, encyclopaedia entry, review article) to build knowledge before tackling a specialist text
Identifies when a comprehension problem stems from missing concepts rather than from unknown words
Recognises when prior beliefs are distorting their reading, for example by attributing to the author a claim the text does not make
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before giving a specialist text, ask the learner to write three things they know and two questions they have about its topic; after reading, ask what the author claimed. Check whether prior knowledge was used to anticipate and check, and whether any 'recalled' content actually came from the learner's beliefs rather than from the text.

topics.name: Managing reading load
topics.description: Plan and triage the reading that university study generates: distinguish essential from further reading, decide what to read closely, partially or not at all in relation to teaching sessions and assessments, and schedule reading realistically given one's own reading rate in English. Effective triage is a judgement about relevance rather than a speed technique, and it involves accepting that not every item on a list is meant to be read in full.
masteryEvidence: Classifies a module reading list into essential, recommended and optional items and justifies the classification from module documents
Estimates the time a reading will take from its length and their own measured rate for that kind of text
Produces a weekly reading plan aligned with lectures, seminars and assessment deadlines
Reads selectively (for example, introduction, conclusion and one relevant section) when the purpose allows, and records what was not read
Revises the plan when it proves unrealistic rather than abandoning reading altogether
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a realistic week's reading (two chapters, three articles, one report) and the week's seminar question, and ask for a reading plan with time estimates. Check whether priorities follow from the seminar question, whether estimates reflect the learner's actual rate, and whether partial reading is planned deliberately rather than happening by default.

topics.name: Reading on screen
topics.description: Read academic texts on screen, as PDFs, e-books and web pages, in ways that sustain comprehension: choosing screen or paper for the task, using search and digital annotation purposefully, managing hyperlinks, tabs and notifications, and checking unfamiliar web sources before trusting them. Meta-analytic evidence suggests a small comprehension disadvantage for screen reading of expository text, particularly under time pressure, which appears to reflect shallower processing and overconfidence rather than the screen as such.
masteryEvidence: Uses PDF tools (search, highlighting, comments, bookmarks) in support of a stated reading purpose rather than as a substitute for processing
Chooses print or a distraction-reduced screen setting for texts that require close, sustained reading
Manages hyperlinks and tabs so that following links serves the purpose and returns to the main text
Checks comprehension after screen reading with a brief unaided summary rather than relying on the feeling of having read
Identifies when a web text needs checking against other sources before it is relied on
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to read a three-page article as a PDF on their own device with a specific question to answer, then to close the file and write a three-sentence answer. Review their annotations alongside the answer: heavy highlighting with a weak answer suggests annotation is replacing processing; a strong answer from sparse, purposeful notes indicates control.

topics.name: Strategic use of first language and translation in reading
topics.description: Use the first language and other languages, bilingual dictionaries, glossaries and machine translation to support comprehension of difficult academic texts while continuing to process the English text itself, verifying key terms and disciplinary meanings, and staying within institutional rules. Reading ability and academic concepts developed in another language are a transferable resource; the risks lie in translation replacing engagement with English, mistranslated technical terms and the loss of hedging, negation and attribution.
masteryEvidence: Uses L1 resources or machine translation selectively for passages that block comprehension, after first attempting them in English
Checks translated key terms against English-language glossaries or disciplinary sources and corrects mistranslations
Compares a machine translation with the English original to verify that hedges, negation and attributions have survived
Draws on L1 reading or subject knowledge to build background for an English text, and records English equivalents of key concepts
Explains what their programme permits regarding translation tools in reading and in submitted work
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 150-word hedged, technical paragraph and ask them to machine-translate it into a language they know well, then explain in English any places where the translation changes a claim's strength, its attribution or a technical term. Strong readers find and explain at least one such shift; weak readers treat the translation as equivalent.

topics.name: Previewing and surveying
topics.description: Survey a text before reading it in detail by examining its title, abstract or summary, headings, introduction and conclusion, figures and section structure, in order to predict content, judge relevance and plan how to read. Previewing builds a framework that makes later careful reading faster and more accurate, and is the quickest reliable way to decide whether a source deserves more time.
masteryEvidence: Predicts the topic, purpose and probable main claim of an article from its title, abstract and headings, and checks the predictions after reading
Decides within a few minutes whether a source is relevant to a given question and justifies the decision
Identifies the type of text (empirical article, review, textbook chapter, report) from preview features
Plans which sections to read closely on the basis of the preview
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an unfamiliar article and three minutes to preview it without reading the body text. Ask for the topic, the type of text, the probable main claim and which section they would read first for a given question. Compare their answers with the article; strong previewers use several features, not only the title.

topics.name: Skimming for gist
topics.description: Read rapidly and selectively, sampling headings, the opening and closing sentences of paragraphs and salient words, to grasp the gist and overall structure of a text. Skimming is useful for orientation and relevance decisions, but it inevitably reduces comprehension of what is skipped, so it complements rather than replaces careful reading of texts that matter for the task.
masteryEvidence: States the gist and overall structure of a 1,000–2,000-word text after a short timed skim
Identifies after skimming which sections contain the information needed for a task
Explains what kind of information skimming loses and decides when a text must be read carefully instead
Samples paragraph-initial and paragraph-final sentences and discourse signals efficiently while skimming
topics.assessmentPrompt: Allow four minutes for a 1,500-word article and ask for its gist in two sentences plus a section-by-section outline; then ask about a qualification stated mid-paragraph. Expect an accurate gist and outline; the final question tests whether the learner recognises the limits of skimming and says that part would need careful reading.

topics.name: Scanning for specific information
topics.description: Locate specific information such as names, dates, figures, terms or a particular claim by searching for its likely form rather than reading continuously, then read the surrounding text carefully to confirm that it answers the question. In academic work scanning is used with indexes, tables, reference lists and long documents, increasingly through digital search, so anticipating wording and verifying context matter more than raw speed.
masteryEvidence: Locates specified items in a long text, table or index quickly and accurately
Anticipates the form the target will take, including synonyms and word-family variants of the search term
Reads the sentence around a located item to confirm that it answers the question rather than merely matching a word
Uses digital search, indexes and contents pages to scan efficiently
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to find, in a ten-page report, three items whose wording in the question is paraphrased in the text (for example 'the proportion of respondents who…'). Check speed, accuracy and whether they verified the context rather than stopping at the first keyword match.

topics.name: Identifying main ideas and supporting detail
topics.description: Identify the central claims of a paragraph, section and whole text and distinguish them from elaboration, examples, evidence and background. Main-idea identification underpins summarising, note-making and critical reading, and in academic texts main ideas are often implicit, distributed across sentences or signalled only through evaluation.
masteryEvidence: States the main idea of a paragraph in their own words, including when it is not expressed in a single topic sentence
Labels sentences in a paragraph by function (claim, explanation, example, evidence, qualification)
Produces a hierarchical outline of a section that separates main points from supporting detail
Identifies the overall thesis or main finding of an article and the sections that state it
Explains why a vivid example or striking statistic is supporting rather than central
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 250-word paragraph whose main idea is implicit or stated mid-paragraph, opening with a memorable example. Ask for the main idea in one sentence of their own. Weak responses restate the example or copy the first sentence; strong responses generalise accurately from the paragraph as a whole.

topics.name: Using paragraph structure when reading
topics.description: Use knowledge of how academic paragraphs are built (controlling sentences, development patterns such as definition, exemplification, cause–effect and comparison, and concluding or linking sentences) to predict and follow paragraph content. Paragraph structure is a probabilistic cue rather than a rule: many expert paragraphs open with background or a counter-view and have delayed, implicit or multiple points.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the controlling sentence of a paragraph when there is one and recognises when there is none
Names the development pattern of a paragraph and the signals that mark it
Predicts a paragraph's likely continuation from its opening sentence and checks the prediction
Recognises transitional and concluding sentences that link a paragraph to its neighbours
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner four academic paragraphs with their sentences jumbled and ask them to reorder each, identifying the controlling sentence and the development pattern. Include one paragraph whose point is stated at the end. Check whether they rely solely on 'the first sentence is the main idea' or use reference and connectors to reconstruct the logic.

topics.name: Recognising text organisation
topics.description: Recognise the overall organisation of a text (problem–solution, claim–counterclaim, general–specific, comparison, cause–effect, chronological) and the signals that mark it (headings, frame markers, signalling nouns, connectors) in order to follow the writer's plan, anticipate what comes next and recall content in structured form. Explicit awareness of top-level structure has been shown to support L2 readers' recall.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the top-level pattern of an article or chapter and the sections that realise each element
Points to the lexical signals of pattern elements, such as 'a major difficulty', 'one response has been', 'this approach fails to'
Builds an outline or graphic organiser of a text from its identified structure
Recalls text content organised by its structure rather than as an unordered list of points
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 600–800-word problem–solution or claim–counterclaim text and a blank graphic organiser for the pattern. Ask the learner to complete it and underline the words that signalled each element. Check the accuracy of the mapping and whether it rests on signals rather than guesswork.

topics.name: Navigating research articles
topics.description: Read empirical research articles non-linearly and efficiently by using their conventional structure (abstract; introduction establishing a gap and aims; methods; results; discussion; conclusion) and their figures and tables to locate what a given purpose requires. Experienced readers rarely read research articles from start to finish; knowing what each section typically does, and how this varies across disciplines and article types, lets novices do the same.
masteryEvidence: States the typical function of each IMRaD section and where gaps, aims, findings and limitations are usually found
Locates the research question, design, sample or data, main findings and acknowledged limitations of an unfamiliar article within a set time
Chooses a reading route suited to the purpose, for example abstract–figures–discussion to judge relevance, or methods–results to evaluate a claim
Recognises disciplinary and article-type variants (combined results and discussion, theory sections, qualitative or review articles without IMRaD) and adapts navigation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an unfamiliar empirical article from the learner's field and ten minutes. Ask them to complete a grid (research question, design, participants or data, main finding, one stated limitation) with the section and page for each. Check accuracy and whether they navigated directly rather than reading from the first line.

topics.name: Making inferences
topics.description: Draw the inferences a text requires but does not state: bridging inferences that connect sentences (cause, contrast, reference), knowledge-based inferences that connect the text to what the reader knows, and inferences about implications and the writer's unstated position. Compressed academic phrasing leaves many logical relations implicit, so inferencing is essential, but inferences must be anchored in textual evidence and revised when the text contradicts them.
masteryEvidence: Supplies the implicit logical relation between two sentences and names the textual evidence for it
States a reasonable implication of a finding or argument that the writer does not spell out
Distinguishes inferences supported by the text from personal speculation or opinion
Revises an inference when later text contradicts it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short passage and three statements: one explicitly stated, one validly inferable and one plausible but unsupported. Ask the learner to classify each and quote the words that justify the decision. Strong readers separate the inferable from the unsupported and point to evidence for both judgements.

topics.name: Tracking reference while reading
topics.description: Resolve reference across sentences while reading: pronouns, demonstratives (this, these, such), signalling and shell nouns (this approach, the problem, these findings), comparative reference (the former, other studies) and substitution or ellipsis. Academic writers often use 'this' plus a summarising noun to encapsulate whole stretches of preceding text, and wrongly resolved reference is a frequent, often unnoticed source of misunderstanding.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the antecedents of pronouns and demonstratives accurately, including when the antecedent is a clause or paragraph
States what a signalling noun such as 'this tendency' or 'these limitations' encapsulates
Traces a chain of repetitions, synonyms and general nouns referring to one key concept through a passage
Detects ambiguous reference and states the most plausible reading with reasons
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 200-word passage with five numbered reference items (two pronouns, two 'this/these + noun' items and one 'the former'). Ask the learner to write what each refers to. Check the encapsulating items especially closely: they require summarising earlier text rather than pointing to a single noun.

topics.name: Distinguishing fact, opinion, claim and evidence
topics.description: Classify statements in academic texts by their epistemic status: background treated as established, the writer's own claim, a claim attributed to others, evidence offered in support, evaluation, and speculation. The school-level fact/opinion binary is inadequate for academic reading, because most academic statements are claims supported to different degrees and marked as such by hedges, boosters and attribution.
masteryEvidence: Labels sentences in an academic paragraph as background, claim, evidence, evaluation or speculation and justifies each label
Identifies the hedges and boosters that signal the strength of a claim
Distinguishes the evidence offered for a claim from the claim itself
Explains why a statement treated as established in one source may be presented as contestable in another
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph containing a hedged claim, a cited statistic, an evaluative sentence and a background statement. Ask the learner to label each and highlight the words that informed their decision. Check whether they move beyond fact versus opinion and use hedging and attribution as cues.

topics.name: Identifying writer stance and attributed views
topics.description: Track whose voice is speaking at each point in an academic text and how strongly the writer endorses, distances themselves from or rejects attributed views, using reporting verbs, attribution, hedges, boosters, attitude markers and concessive structures as cues. Attributing a cited view to the writer, or missing the writer's evaluation of a source, is a common cause of misrepresentation in student summaries and essays.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes the writer's own claims from views attributed to other sources
Interprets the evaluative force of reporting verbs and frames (demonstrates versus claims versus suggests; 'X argues…, yet…')
Identifies concessive structures in which the writer acknowledges a view before rejecting or qualifying it
States the writer's overall position in a debate and the textual evidence for it
Summarises a passage while preserving who said what and with what degree of commitment
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 300-word literature-review paragraph that reports three sources and evaluates one critically. Ask which view the writer holds, which they reject and how the learner knows. Check whether cited views are attributed correctly and whether the learner points to reporting verbs, concession and evaluative language as evidence.

topics.name: Monitoring comprehension
topics.description: Notice while reading when comprehension has broken down or is too shallow for the purpose, diagnose the likely cause and apply a matching repair: rereading, slowing down, reading on for clarification, parsing a sentence, checking a key word, consulting a background source or asking a question. Monitoring is a metacognitive skill, and readers often overestimate their understanding, especially of difficult or unfamiliar texts.
masteryEvidence: Marks points of breakdown during reading and labels their likely cause
Selects a repair matched to the cause and reports whether it worked
Generates and answers self-questions to test understanding at the end of each section
Detects an inserted inconsistency or contradiction in a text
Predicts their own comprehension score with reasonable accuracy
topics.assessmentPrompt: Insert into a 400-word text one sentence that contradicts an earlier claim. Ask the learner to read and note anything confusing, rate their understanding from 1 to 5 and answer four questions. Check whether they detected the inconsistency and how closely their rating matched their score.

topics.name: Purposeful annotation
topics.description: Annotate texts selectively and in one's own words, marking main claims, structure, key evidence, questions and links to a task, so that annotations support later summary, discussion or writing. Annotation helps to the extent that it requires processing; extensive highlighting without comment has low utility for learning, and annotations that do not separate the author's ideas from the reader's create risks for later source use.
masteryEvidence: Annotates with a small set of consistent codes or colours whose meanings are defined in advance
Writes brief margin summaries of paragraph points and notes questions or disagreements in their own words
Distinguishes in annotations between the author's claims, views the author reports and their own responses
Uses their annotations to produce a summary or answer a task question without rereading the whole text
topics.assessmentPrompt: Collect a learner's annotated copy of a recent reading and ask them to answer a question about the text using only their annotations. Check how much of the text is highlighted, whether there are own-word comments and whether the annotations are sufficient to answer the question.

topics.name: Reading textbooks
topics.description: Read introductory textbooks to learn disciplinary content, using their apparatus (chapter objectives, headings, definitions, worked examples, figures, summaries, review questions) to organise study and to check learning through self-testing. Textbooks are the main reading genre in many foundation and first-year programmes, and their dense definitions, taxonomies and technical explanations make them demanding despite their pedagogical design.
masteryEvidence: Uses chapter objectives and summaries to preview and review a chapter
Extracts definitions and builds a glossary or concept map showing how key terms relate
Answers end-of-chapter or self-generated questions without looking back, then checks and corrects answers
Follows a worked example or process explanation step by step and explains it in their own words
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a four-to-six-page textbook section. After reading, ask the learner, without the text, to define three key terms, explain one relationship between concepts and answer one application question. Check accuracy and whether definitions reflect the textbook's meaning rather than everyday senses of the words.

topics.name: Integrating text and visuals
topics.description: Integrate information from figures, tables and diagrams with the surrounding prose: follow references to visuals, consult them at the point they are needed, check whether the writer's description matches what they show, and notice what they show that the text does not mention. Many readers skip visuals or read them superficially, missing evidence on which the argument depends.
masteryEvidence: Locates the visual a passage refers to and states what it is meant to show
Checks a writer's verbal claim about a figure or table against the data and identifies any overstatement
Identifies a pattern or exception in a visual that the text does not mention
Explains how a diagram or conceptual model relates to the prose account of a process or framework
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a results paragraph with an accompanying graph or table in which one textual claim slightly overstates the data. Ask whether the text describes the visual accurately. Check whether the learner consults the visual closely and identifies the specific mismatch.

dependencies.reason: Evaluating a text presupposes accurate comprehension of what it claims
Critical reading applies a view of critical thinking as questioning and evaluation, including its contested and disciplinary character
Finding an argument in a text requires knowing what counts as an academic argument as opposed to a topic or a list of facts
Reasons, conclusions and counter-arguments are often signalled by causal and contrastive connectors
Evidence can only be judged relevant or sufficient relative to the claim it is offered for
Judging evidence in a text applies knowledge of evidence types and their strengths and limits
Unstated premises are identified as gaps in an argument that has first been reconstructed
The concept of a warrant provides the main tool for naming assumptions that link evidence to claims
Surfacing assumptions is a form of inference about what a writer takes for granted
Recognising perspective builds on identifying the writer's stance and how other voices are framed
Perspective is often carried by value assumptions and framings
Selective use of evidence is a key indicator of perspective and must be distinguished from legitimate selection
Critiquing methods requires locating design, sample, measures and limitations within research articles
Methods critique applies general evidence evaluation to the specific question of what a study design can show
Evaluating quantitative studies requires a consumer-level understanding of significance, confidence intervals and effect sizes
Comparing and corroborating across texts requires identifying each text's claims and support
Weighing conflicting claims draws on evaluating each source's authority, currency and purpose
Tracking which source holds which view across texts depends on reading attribution and stance accurately within each text
Reading priorities are derived from an analysis of the assignment question, scope and criteria
Reading for a task applies triage and planning to the sources an assignment requires
Usable task-oriented reading depends on notes that record source details and separate quotation, paraphrase and comment
Mapping a literature scales up comparison and integration across texts to a whole body of work
Following citations backwards and forwards reveals influential works and lines of debate
Mapping a large literature requires triaging what to read closely and what to note only in outline
Theoretical prose relies on long, abstract, nominalised sentences that must be parsed accurately
Reconstructing a theoretical argument applies argument identification at a high level of abstraction
Theoretical texts give everyday words such as power, culture or structure specialised senses that readers must recognise
Critical question sets operationalise an understanding of what critical reading involves
Text-specific critical questions build on a general habit of asking how, why and with what evidence
Questions about claims, reasons and evidence presuppose that these can be located in the text
A reasoned response is built from answers to systematic critical questions about the text
Supporting an evaluative position requires judgements about the text's evidence
The most substantive critical responses often address the assumptions on which an argument rests
Unpacking nominalised processes, and the postmodified noun phrases that carry them, into who-did-what clauses is the core operation in parsing compressed academic prose
Long premodifier strings (noun + noun sequences, participles, adjectives) must be analysed to locate the head noun of academic noun phrases
Automatic recognition presupposes stable form–meaning knowledge of the most frequent word families; words not yet known cannot be recognised fluently
Reading rate is constrained chiefly by the speed of word identification, so rate training builds on automatic recognition of known words
Extensive reading of easy texts supplies the volume of practice from which rate gains emerge; timed and repeated reading then refine them
Choosing texts in which nearly all running words are known applies the lexical coverage principle to text selection
Adjusting reading to purpose rests on understanding comprehension as constructed by the reader to a standard set by their goal
Background knowledge is the knowledge-based component of the interactive model; understanding the model explains why knowledge-building is a reading strategy
Triage decisions about what to read closely, partially or not at all are made relative to the purpose of each reading
Realistic scheduling depends on knowing one's own reading rate for different text types
Reading plans apply general planning and prioritising skills to the specific demands of reading lists
Digital annotation transfers principles of purposeful, selective annotation to PDF and web tools
Countering overconfidence after fast screen reading depends on habits of checking one's own comprehension
Using machine translation to support reading presupposes knowing what MT can and cannot do and what uses are permitted
L1 and translation resources work best as repair strategies chosen after a reader notices a specific breakdown
Previewing serves decisions about relevance and reading approach that only make sense relative to a reading purpose
Previewing works by activating topic and genre knowledge that frames later reading
Skimming extends the survey of preview features into the body of the text
Efficient skimming samples controlling and concluding sentences, relying on knowledge of how paragraphs are built
Skimming at speed depends on rapid recognition of content words
Scanning is defined by a specific information target set by the reading purpose
Scanning requires rapid recognition of target forms and their word-family variants
Identifying central claims within paragraphs draws on recognising controlling sentences and development patterns
Development patterns within paragraphs are signalled partly by connectors
Recognising organisation while reading applies knowledge of problem–solution, claim–counterclaim and related text patterns
Frame markers and advance organisers are the main explicit signals of text structure
Non-linear navigation of articles builds on surveying abstracts, headings and figures
Awareness that texts follow conventional organisations transfers to the IMRaD macrostructure and its variants
Readers need to recognise an empirical article, as opposed to a review or theoretical paper, before applying IMRaD-based navigation
Knowledge-based and many bridging inferences draw directly on the reader's background knowledge
Inferring implications presupposes accurate identification of what is explicitly claimed
Bridging inferences depend on correctly linking referring expressions across sentences
Resolving reference while reading requires knowing how pronouns and demonstratives refer in English
Classifying statements by status presupposes identifying the propositions a paragraph makes and how they relate
Tracking stance requires the distinction between claims the writer makes and claims attributed to others
Judging how strongly a writer commits to a view builds on classifying statements by epistemic status
Concessive structures are where writers acknowledge and then reject or qualify other views, and are the commonest site of misattribution
Monitoring and repair draw on knowledge of oneself as a reader and of the strategies available
What counts as adequate understanding, and therefore as a breakdown, is set by the reading purpose
Selective annotation requires distinguishing central claims from supporting detail
What is worth annotating depends on what the reading is for
Learning from textbook sections requires identifying key concepts and principles among examples and elaboration
Textbook apparatus (objectives, headings, summaries) is used most effectively as a preview and review framework
Textbooks rely heavily on formal definitions and classifications that readers must recognise and unpack
Checking prose against a figure requires reading axes, scales and legends accurately
Many claims in academic texts are supported by tables that must be read row by row and column by column
Reconciling text with a visual requires first identifying the claim the text makes about the data
Finding the main clause of a long sentence means bracketing adverbial and other subordinate clauses and identifying which finite verb belongs to the main clause
Embedded relative clauses separate a head noun from its verb; parsing requires locating where the relative clause begins and ends

guidance.summary: Moore (2013) found that academics in history, philosophy and cultural studies understand critical thinking in at least seven different ways, from judgement and scepticism to sensitive reading and self-reflexivity, and Atkinson (1997) questioned whether it can be taught as a culture-free, generic skill. Wallace and Wray (2016) present critical reading as evaluating texts in relation to the reader's own purpose, with constructive as well as sceptical engagement. Teach critical reading as discipline-situated questioning and evaluation, model it with texts from learners' fields, and make explicit that being critical includes recognising strengths.

activities.title: Description versus evaluation sort
learnerActions: Sort statements about a text into descriptive and evaluative
Rewrite two descriptive statements as evaluations with reasons
Discuss what makes an evaluation 'critical' in your discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Critical reading adds a reasoned judgement to an accurate account of the text.
activities.rationale: Makes explicit the distinction between describing and evaluating that underpins critical reading for postgraduates in Wallace and Wray (2016).

activities.title: What does 'critical' mean here?
learnerActions: Read short extracts of assessment criteria or feedback from different departments that use the word 'critical'
Identify what each seems to mean by it
Compare your findings with the range of meanings academics report
activities.intendedInsight: 'Critical' has different emphases in different disciplines.
activities.rationale: Draws on Moore's (2013) finding of multiple disciplinary meanings to avoid a one-size-fits-all model.

difficulties.pattern: 'Being critical means finding what is wrong.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques that list only weaknesses, often minor ones.
difficulties.response: Model balanced evaluation that includes strengths, and ask what a text does well for a given purpose.

difficulties.pattern: Criticises what they assume the text says rather than what it says.
difficulties.revealedBy: Criticisms of claims the author did not make.
difficulties.response: Require an accurate summary before evaluation, and check comprehension first.

difficulties.pattern: 'Who am I to criticise a published expert?'
difficulties.revealedBy: Purely descriptive responses and reluctance to evaluate.
difficulties.response: Frame critique as participation in an academic conversation, model respectful evaluative language and acknowledge that educational systems differ in how far questioning authorities is expected, without attributing this to learners' cultures.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What is critical reading, and what would it involve for an article in your subject?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes questioning claims, evidence and assumptions relative to a purpose, including strengths, with a discipline-specific example.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes evaluation, but only as finding faults.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates critical reading with careful reading or summary.

guidance.contextNotes: Introduce at foundation level through accessible argumentative texts. Pre-sessional courses should link the concept to assessed tasks. In-sessional and postgraduate teaching should model discipline-specific criticality, ideally with input from subject staff.
reviewNotes: Whether critical thinking should be taught as a generic skill or only within disciplines is contested; this topic takes a disciplinarily situated position.

guidance.summary: Toulmin's (2003) model offers a vocabulary of claim, grounds and warrant that helps readers reconstruct arguments, and Walton (2006) shows how argument structure can be diagrammed and evaluated. Wallace and Wray (2016) stress identifying what an author is claiming and how the claims are supported before judging them. Teach reconstruction through outlines and argument maps, using authentic texts in which arguments are embedded in description and literature review, and check reconstructions for fairness to the author.

activities.title: Claim–reasons–evidence outline
learnerActions: Find the main claim of a text and write it as a contestable statement
List the reasons offered and the evidence for each
Check whether the author would accept your outline as fair
activities.intendedInsight: Arguments have a structure that can be reconstructed and checked.
activities.rationale: Uses the claim–grounds structure from Toulmin (2003) as a reading tool.

activities.title: Argument mapping
learnerActions: Draw a box-and-arrow map of a short argumentative text
Mark co-premises, objections and rebuttals
Compare maps with peers and resolve differences by returning to the text
activities.intendedInsight: Mapping exposes the logical structure of an argument and its gaps.
activities.rationale: Diagramming argument structure is set out in Walton (2006), and van Gelder (2005) argues that practice with argument maps supports critical thinking.

difficulties.pattern: Gives the topic as the claim ('The main claim is climate change').
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines whose 'claim' cannot be agreed or disagreed with.
difficulties.response: Teach that a claim is a statement that could be disputed, and practise turning topics into claims.

difficulties.pattern: Lists evidence as if it were the reasons.
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines in which statistics appear as reasons without a stated point.
difficulties.response: Distinguish claim, reason and evidence with labelled examples from the same text.

difficulties.pattern: Misses the argumentative force of connectors such as thus, however and nevertheless.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions misidentified; counter-arguments read as the author's position.
difficulties.response: Highlight conclusion indicators and contrastive signals before mapping.

diagnostic.task: A claim–reasons–evidence outline of a 500-word argumentative text.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate, complete and fair reconstruction.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The correct claim, but reasons and evidence mixed together.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A topic given as the claim, followed by a list of content.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners work with accessible argumentative texts. In-sessional and PGT learners apply the skill to disciplinary articles, where arguments are embedded in the reporting of research and in literature reviews.

guidance.summary: Kuhn (1991) found that many people struggle to distinguish evidence from theory and to judge how well evidence supports a claim, which suggests that evidence evaluation must be taught explicitly. Gal (2002) argues that statistical literacy includes asking critical questions about where data come from, how they were produced and how they are interpreted. Teach evaluation through explicit criteria (relevance, sufficiency, quality) applied to authentic texts, and aim for calibrated judgements rather than wholesale acceptance or dismissal (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

activities.title: Evidence audit
learnerActions: For each main claim in a text, identify the type of evidence offered
Rate its relevance, sufficiency and quality, giving a reason for each rating
Write a one-sentence judgement of how well the claim is supported overall
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence can be strong for one claim and weak for another in the same text.
activities.rationale: Applies explicit criteria to make evaluation systematic (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

activities.title: Questions for a statistical claim
learnerActions: Read a news report of a study
Ask who collected the data, how, from whom, and whether the headline claim follows
Compare the report with the study's abstract
activities.intendedInsight: Reported statistics need checking against their source and the design behind them.
activities.rationale: Uses the critical questions about data that Gal (2002) treats as part of statistical literacy.

difficulties.pattern: Treats any statistic or citation as strong evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluations that cite the presence of numbers or references as proof.
difficulties.response: Teach evidence types and their typical limits with contrasting examples.

difficulties.pattern: Dismisses evidence as 'biased' or 'not enough' without specific reasons.
difficulties.revealedBy: Blanket scepticism applied equally to all sources.
difficulties.response: Require a specific reason for every negative judgement and a statement of what evidence would be adequate.

difficulties.pattern: Accepts causal claims based on correlational data.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncritical acceptance of 'X leads to Y' drawn from cross-sectional survey data.
difficulties.response: Teach the correlation–causation distinction with field-relevant examples.

diagnostic.task: A short text making a general claim supported by one statistic and one anecdote; ask how well the claim is supported.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notes the mismatch in scope and the limits of each evidence type, and reaches a calibrated judgement.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes one weakness without connecting it to the scope of the claim.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts or dismisses the claim without specific reasons.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners build general criteria. PGT and PGR learners apply the evidential standards of their disciplines, which differ, for example, between experimental sciences, social research and the humanities.

guidance.summary: Toulmin's (2003) warrant names the often unstated principle that licenses the step from evidence to claim, and Walton (2006) treats the reconstruction of missing premises and the critical questions attached to common argument schemes. Teach learners to ask what must be true for a conclusion to follow and to distinguish a missing premise from an objection. Value and framing assumptions deserve explicit attention because they are often naturalised in disciplinary and policy texts (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

activities.title: Find the missing premise
learnerActions: Read a short argument with a gap between its evidence and its conclusion
Write the premise that would close the gap
Judge whether that premise is acceptable
activities.intendedInsight: Many arguments rest on unstated premises, which may be their weakest part.
activities.rationale: Applies the warrant concept (Toulmin, 2003) and missing-premise reconstruction (Walton, 2006).

activities.title: Reframing an issue
learnerActions: Identify how a text frames an issue, for example as an economic, health or rights question
Rewrite the opening paragraph under a different frame
Discuss how the frame changes what counts as relevant evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Framings carry value assumptions that shape the whole argument.
activities.rationale: Makes value assumptions visible as part of critical reading (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

difficulties.pattern: Offers an objection instead of an assumption ('The assumption is that it might not work').
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Assumptions' that are criticisms rather than premises the author relies on.
difficulties.response: Contrast what the author takes for granted with what could go wrong, using the warrant as a model.

difficulties.pattern: Restates the conclusion as the assumption.
difficulties.revealedBy: Circular 'assumptions' that repeat the claim.
difficulties.response: Test each proposed assumption by asking whether the argument fails without it, starting from a clear reconstruction of the argument.

difficulties.pattern: Finds assumptions only in texts they disagree with.
difficulties.revealedBy: Detailed analysis of uncongenial texts and none of congenial ones.
difficulties.response: Deliberately set texts aligned with learners' own views and use peer questioning.

diagnostic.task: A short argument with an implicit premise; the learner states the premise.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a genuine missing premise and evaluates its acceptability.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Points towards the premise but states it vaguely.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the claim or raises an objection.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners practise with accessible policy and argumentative texts. PGT and PGR learners extend the skill to theoretical and paradigmatic assumptions in research.

guidance.summary: All texts are written from a position, so the aim is not to label texts 'biased' but to understand how perspective shapes selection, framing and language and to judge the consequences for reliability. Wineburg and McGrew (2019) show that professional fact-checkers establish who is behind an unfamiliar source before reading it closely, and Nickerson (1998) reviews how confirmation bias shapes readers' own evaluations. Teach both directions: perspective in the text and bias in the reader.

activities.title: Same issue, two sources
learnerActions: Read two texts on one issue from organisations with different interests
Compare their terminology, the evidence each selects and what each omits
Write a balanced account noting how each perspective shapes the text
activities.intendedInsight: Perspective shows in concrete choices that can be identified without dismissing a source.
activities.rationale: Develops analysis of framing and selection as part of critical reading (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

activities.title: Who is behind this?
learnerActions: Before reading an unfamiliar web source closely, search for information about its author or organisation
Note funding, mission and affiliations
Read the source and discuss how this information affects your evaluation
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing who produced a text helps interpret its perspective.
activities.rationale: Based on the lateral reading practices of professional fact-checkers (Wineburg & McGrew, 2019).

difficulties.pattern: 'This text is biased, so it is useless.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Sources dismissed on the basis of affiliation alone.
difficulties.response: Distinguish perspective from distortion and evaluate the evidence on its merits.

difficulties.pattern: Recognises bias only in texts they disagree with.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncritical acceptance of congenial sources.
difficulties.response: Discuss confirmation bias explicitly and ask learners to evaluate a text they agree with.

difficulties.pattern: Misses perspective expressed through framing rather than explicit opinion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements that a text is neutral because it never says 'I think'.
difficulties.response: Analyse framing, lexical choice and the treatment of other voices.

diagnostic.task: Two texts on one issue; ask about framing, evidence selection and omissions in each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies specific framing, selection and omissions in both texts.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies perspective in only one text.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Labels one text biased without evidence.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners focus on public, media and policy texts. PGT learners extend the analysis to research funding, researcher positionality and paradigms.

guidance.summary: Methods critique asks whether a study's design can support its conclusions. Creswell and Creswell (2018) set out the logic of quantitative, qualitative and mixed designs, Gal (2002) frames statistical literacy as asking critical questions about data, and Wasserstein and Lazar (2016) caution against equating statistical significance with importance or truth. Teach a consumer-level set of questions adapted separately to quantitative and qualitative studies, practise with studies from learners' fields, and involve subject specialists where possible.

activities.title: Design–claim match
learnerActions: Read a study's abstract and methods section
Identify the design, sample and measures
Judge whether the conclusion matches what the design can show and suggest a better-calibrated conclusion
activities.intendedInsight: Conclusions should not go beyond what the design can support.
activities.rationale: Applies the logic of research design (Creswell & Creswell, 2018) to reading.

activities.title: Significance versus importance
learnerActions: Read a results paragraph reporting p-values and effect sizes
Explain in plain words what the numbers indicate
Discuss whether the finding matters in practice
activities.intendedInsight: A statistically significant result may be small or unimportant, and a non-significant one is not proof of no effect.
activities.rationale: Draws on the principles in the ASA statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).

difficulties.pattern: Applies quantitative criteria to qualitative studies ('the sample is too small to be valid').
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques of qualitative studies focused solely on sample size and generalisability.
difficulties.response: Teach criteria appropriate to qualitative research and discuss the different aims of the two traditions.

difficulties.pattern: Bases critique on the abstract because methods information cannot be found.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic critiques that could apply to any study.
difficulties.response: Practise locating design information in methods sections and appendices.

difficulties.pattern: Equates statistical significance with importance or proof.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements such as 'the study proves…' based on p < .05.
difficulties.response: Teach basic interpretation of significance, effect size and confidence intervals.

diagnostic.task: The abstract and methods of a study whose conclusion over-generalises; ask whether the conclusion is justified.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Connects specific design features to the scope of the claim and proposes a calibrated conclusion.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes a limitation but does not connect it to the conclusion.
