diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts the conclusion as stated.

guidance.contextNotes: Undergraduates in empirical disciplines meet this in later years. PGT learners need it for literature reviews and dissertations. PGR learners need discipline-specific critique; EAP input should complement, not replace, research methods training.
reviewNotes: EAP practitioners may lack expertise in specific research methods; collaboration with subject staff is advisable. The EGAP classification reflects consumer-level critique; specialist appraisal is discipline-specific.

guidance.summary: Multiple-text comprehension involves constructing a representation of both the content of several documents and the sources themselves and their relationships (Perfetti et al., 1999). Bråten et al. (2009) found that students' trust in and evaluation of sources related to how well they understood an issue across multiple texts, and Spivey (1990) describes discourse synthesis as selecting, organising and connecting content from several sources. Teach sourcing explicitly, use sets of texts that genuinely conflict, and require attributed integration rather than serial summaries.

activities.title: Source-tagged comparison grid
learnerActions: Read three texts on an issue
Complete a grid of claims, each tagged with its source details
Mark agreement, conflict or difference of focus across the texts
activities.intendedInsight: Integrating texts requires tracking who said what, not only what was said.
activities.rationale: Supports construction of a representation that links content to sources (Perfetti et al., 1999) and attention to sources (Bråten et al., 2009).

activities.title: Explaining disagreement
learnerActions: Identify a conflict between two sources
Investigate possible reasons: method, sample, definitions, date, perspective
Write an account that explains the conflict rather than merely reporting it
activities.intendedInsight: Conflicts between sources often have explanations that matter for synthesis.
activities.rationale: Develops the connecting operations of discourse synthesis (Spivey, 1990).

difficulties.pattern: Ignores source information and treats all texts as equally reliable.
difficulties.revealedBy: Integrated accounts that never mention authors, dates or publication venues.
difficulties.response: Require sourcing notes for every text and discuss how source features affect trust.

difficulties.pattern: Summarises each text separately without comparing them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Serial summaries with no cross-reference.
difficulties.response: Use comparison grids and integration prompts that require each point to draw on at least two sources.

difficulties.pattern: Assumes that if sources disagree, one of them must simply be wrong.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accounts that declare a winner without considering method or scope.
difficulties.response: Explore legitimate reasons for disagreement and discuss knowledge as constructed and contested.

diagnostic.task: Three partly conflicting texts; ask for a brief integrated account.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An attributed integration that explains the conflicts.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A comparison that identifies conflicts but does not explain them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Serial summaries without attribution or comparison.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can introduce multiple-text reading with sets of short texts. Undergraduate in-sessional learners apply it to assignments. PGT and PGR learners need it at scale for literature reviews.

guidance.summary: Studies of university tasks show that much assessed writing draws on reading sources (Horowitz, 1986; Leki & Carson, 1997), and Grabe and Zhang (2013) argue for teaching reading and writing together in EAP. Plakans and Gebril (2012) show that writers in integrated tasks use sources for ideas, organisation and language. Teach reading as driven by the question, with notes organised by the writer's emerging points, and integrate reading tasks with writing assignments rather than teaching them separately (Hirvela, 2004).

activities.title: Question-driven reading plan
learnerActions: Break an essay question into sub-questions
Map each sub-question to likely sources and sections
Read and take notes under sub-question headings
activities.intendedInsight: Reading for writing is organised by the question, not by the source.
activities.rationale: Integrates reading and writing in line with Grabe and Zhang (2013) and Hirvela (2004).

activities.title: From notes to paragraph
learnerActions: Use notes from three sources to plan one paragraph
Check that your notes distinguish quotation, paraphrase and own comment
Write the paragraph and reflect on any gaps in your reading
activities.intendedInsight: How you read and take notes determines how easily and how honestly you can write.
activities.rationale: Reflects the reading-to-write processes observed in integrated tasks (Plakans & Gebril, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Reads everything on the topic before deciding what the question requires.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large volumes of notes, many irrelevant to the question.
difficulties.response: Begin with question analysis and set reading priorities before reading.

difficulties.pattern: Copies source wording into notes without marking it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Patchwriting in drafts traceable to unmarked notes.
difficulties.response: Teach note conventions that distinguish quotation, paraphrase and comment. Treat early patchwriting as developmental rather than as misconduct.

difficulties.pattern: Expects to write from personal opinion and general knowledge, as in many test and school essay tasks.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments with few sources and much unsupported assertion.
difficulties.response: Use source-based writing tasks from the start of a course and make the expectation of source use explicit.

diagnostic.task: An essay question and five sources; ask which to use and how to organise notes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Question-driven selection and a note plan organised by points.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Relevant selection but notes planned source by source.
diagnostic.gapResponse: All sources treated equally, or selection unrelated to the question.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses should use source-based assessments. In-sessional undergraduates and PGT students apply the skill to disciplinary assignments and dissertations.

guidance.summary: Feak and Swales (2009) treat the literature review as a research story in which writers position their work; mapping the literature is its reading counterpart. Kwan (2006) describes the thematic organisation of doctoral literature reviews, and the ACRL (2016) frame of scholarship as conversation captures the idea that sources respond to one another over time. Teach mapping as iterative, visual and conceptual, using concept maps or matrices and citation networks.

activities.title: Concept map of a literature
learnerActions: Write each source on a card or digital note
Group the cards by theme or position and draw the relationships between groups
Mark debates and areas with little research
activities.intendedInsight: A literature has a structure beyond the list of its sources.
activities.rationale: Constructing concept maps is associated with better learning than studying text alone (Nesbit & Adesope, 2006), and the map makes the scholarly conversation visible (ACRL, 2016).

activities.title: Following the conversation
learnerActions: Take an influential article and find works that cite it
Note how later works build on, extend or challenge it
Add these relationships to your map
activities.intendedInsight: Fields develop through dialogue between texts over time.
activities.rationale: Links mapping to positioning one's own work within a research story (Feak & Swales, 2009).

difficulties.pattern: Organises the map source by source rather than by theme or position.
difficulties.revealedBy: Maps that are annotated lists.
difficulties.response: Prompt grouping by theme or position and require at least one relationship between groups.

difficulties.pattern: Feels overwhelmed by the volume of literature and keeps searching without mapping.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ever-growing reference lists with no organising structure.
difficulties.response: Set boundaries for the search, start from review articles and map early.

difficulties.pattern: Misses the influential works on which a field builds.
difficulties.revealedBy: Maps containing only recent articles.
difficulties.response: Use backward and forward citation chaining to identify frequently cited works.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to map ten sources on their topic.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Conceptual grouping with debates, relationships and gaps visible.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Thematic grouping without relationships between groups.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A list of sources.

guidance.contextNotes: Final-year undergraduates use mapping for dissertations. PGT learners need it for literature reviews; PGR researchers use it continuously to position their research and update their understanding of the field.

guidance.summary: Maton's (2013) concepts of semantic gravity and semantic density describe how theoretical texts operate at high abstraction and condensation, and how understanding involves moving between abstract concepts and concrete cases ('semantic waves'). Meyer and Land (2005) describe threshold concepts as potentially troublesome knowledge that learners may grasp only after a period of confusion. Teach the reading of theory through concept glossaries, plain-language reconstructions and example generation, and normalise multiple readings.

activities.title: Riding the semantic wave
learnerActions: Identify an abstract claim in a theoretical extract
Find or create a concrete example of it
Restate the claim in plain language and link it back to the theory's terms
activities.intendedInsight: Understanding theory involves moving back and forth between the abstract and the concrete.
activities.rationale: Based on the concept of semantic waves (Maton, 2013).

activities.title: Theory glossary
learnerActions: List key terms with the author's own definition of each
Note how each differs from everyday use
Compare with another theorist's use of the same term
activities.intendedInsight: Theory-specific meanings of familiar words need explicit attention.
activities.rationale: Addresses the troublesome character of threshold concepts (Meyer & Land, 2005).

difficulties.pattern: Reads theoretical terms such as discourse, capital or structure in their everyday sense.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misinterpretations that make sense only with the everyday meaning.
difficulties.response: Build theory glossaries and contrast everyday and theoretical senses explicitly.

difficulties.pattern: Gets lost in long, abstract, nominalised sentences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inability to restate the claim of a key sentence.
difficulties.response: Parse key sentences together and unpack nominalisations.

difficulties.pattern: Cannot see what the text is arguing against.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that present the theory without its position in a debate.
difficulties.response: Identify the opposing position the author constructs and how the argument responds to it.

diagnostic.task: A theoretical extract; ask for definitions of two concepts, a restatement of the argument and an example.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Faithful definitions, an accurate argument and an apt example.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate definitions but a vague account of the argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Everyday definitions and no identifiable argument.

guidance.contextNotes: Undergraduates in the humanities and social sciences meet theoretical texts early. PGT and PGR learners face extended theoretical reading, often of works translated from other languages, where translators' terminological choices add a further layer.

guidance.summary: Walton (2006) pairs common argumentation schemes, such as argument from expert opinion or from analogy, with critical questions that test them, and Wallace and Wray (2016) propose a set of critical synopsis questions to guide postgraduate reading. Reciprocal teaching illustrates the value of questioning routines that are modelled and then handed over to learners (Palincsar & Brown, 1984). Teach a compact question set, model its use, and encourage learners to adapt it to their discipline and purpose.

activities.title: Applying a question set
learnerActions: Apply a five-question set covering purpose, claims, evidence, assumptions and usefulness to a short text
Answer each question with references to the text
Discuss which questions were most productive for this text
activities.intendedInsight: Systematic questions make critical reading manageable and focused.
activities.rationale: Adapts the critical synopsis approach of Wallace and Wray (2016).

activities.title: Scheme-specific questions
learnerActions: Identify an argument from expert opinion or from analogy in a text
Apply the critical questions associated with that type of argument
Judge the argument's strength
activities.intendedInsight: Different kinds of argument invite different critical questions.
activities.rationale: Based on argumentation schemes and their critical questions (Walton, 2006).

difficulties.pattern: Asks only comprehension questions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions that can be answered by locating information in the text.
difficulties.response: Model evaluative questions and contrast them with comprehension questions on the same text.

difficulties.pattern: Applies the question set mechanically, regardless of text or purpose.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uniform, formulaic answers across very different texts.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to choose and adapt the questions most relevant to their purpose and discipline.

diagnostic.task: Ask for five questions about a short text and answers to two of them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Questions address claims, evidence, assumptions and implications, with text-based answers.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A mix of comprehension and evaluative questions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Comprehension questions only.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners can use simplified question sets with accessible texts. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners use them for seminar preparation and critiques. Doctoral researchers adapt them to the norms of their field.

guidance.summary: A critical response draws on an evaluativist view of knowledge, in which claims are weighed by evidence and argument rather than accepted as certain or dismissed as mere opinion (Hofer & Pintrich, 1997). Wallace and Wray (2016) and Swales and Feak (2012) treat critique as reasoned evaluation grounded in analysis of the text. Teach critical response through structured tasks that move from summary to analysis to evaluation, with models of qualified evaluative language.

activities.title: Summary–analysis–evaluation ladder
learnerActions: Write a two-sentence summary of the text
Identify two features of its argument or evidence
Evaluate each feature with a reason
Combine these into a short response that takes a position
activities.intendedInsight: A critical response is built on an accurate summary and specific analysis.
activities.rationale: Structures the move from comprehension to evaluation (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

activities.title: Test your response in discussion
learnerActions: Prepare a position on a reading for a seminar
Present it with reasons and respond to challenges from peers
Revise your position in writing afterwards
activities.intendedInsight: Critical responses are tested and refined through dialogue.
activities.rationale: Evaluativist thinking involves weighing and revising views in light of argument and evidence (Hofer & Pintrich, 1997).

difficulties.pattern: Gives a personal opinion unconnected to the text ('I agree because it is important').
difficulties.revealedBy: Responses whose reasons do not refer to the text's argument or evidence.
difficulties.response: Require each reason to be linked to a specific feature of the text.

difficulties.pattern: Summarises at length and adds a one-line evaluation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Responses dominated by summary.
difficulties.response: Limit the summary to a fixed length and scaffold the evaluation with critical questions.

difficulties.pattern: 'Everyone has their own opinion, so all views are equally valid.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Refusal to take a position, or conclusions that simply list views.
difficulties.response: Discuss how academic judgements weigh evidence and argument, and model qualified positions.

diagnostic.task: A 150-word response to a short argumentative article.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A qualified position supported by text-linked reasons, acknowledging strengths and limitations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A position supported by general rather than text-specific reasons.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A summary, or an unsupported opinion.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners practise through summary–response tasks. In-sessional learners write critiques and reviews of articles. Doctoral researchers apply the skill in literature reviews and peer review.

guidance.summary: Introduce the interactive model through learners' own reading experiences rather than as theory for its own sake; the goal is diagnostic self-awareness. Grabe's (2009) synthesis shows that efficient lower-level processing is a precondition for higher-level comprehension, and meta-analytic evidence indicates that L2 vocabulary and grammar knowledge correlate more strongly with L2 reading comprehension than L1 reading ability or strategy knowledge do (Jeon & Yamashita, 2014), consistent with Alderson's (1984) language-threshold argument. Keep the model simple (words, sentences, what the text says, what the reader understands) and return to it whenever learners report difficulty.

activities.title: Reading breakdown log
learnerActions: Read a short academic text at your own pace and mark every point where understanding faltered
For each mark, decide whether the cause was an unknown word, a sentence you could not untangle, a missing link between ideas or unfamiliar subject matter
Compare logs in pairs and agree one remedy for each cause type
activities.intendedInsight: Different breakdowns have different causes and need different responses; reading strategies cannot compensate for every problem.
activities.rationale: Making lower- and higher-level processes visible helps learners locate problems instead of attributing all difficulty to the text or to themselves; the cause categories mirror the component-skills view in Grabe (2009).

activities.title: Same text, more knowledge
learnerActions: Read a specialist paragraph once with no preparation and write a two-sentence summary
Read a short accessible introduction to the same topic
Reread the paragraph, summarise again and compare what the background reading made possible
activities.intendedInsight: What the reader brings to the text changes what they can take from it, even when the language is unchanged.
activities.rationale: Demonstrates the knowledge-based contribution to comprehension that construction–integration models describe (Kintsch, 1998) and that Grabe and Stoller (2011) build into reading pedagogy.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I learn the right strategies, I will be able to understand any text.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners apply previewing or skimming routines to texts whose vocabulary is far beyond them and still cannot answer basic questions.
difficulties.response: Show, using an estimate of unknown-word density in the learner's own text, that strategies operate on language that is already largely understood, and redirect effort towards vocabulary and fluency alongside strategy work. Do not abandon strategy teaching; present it as dependent on a language base.

difficulties.pattern: 'I understood every word but I don't know what it means.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate word-level glosses but summaries that list details without a central point.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a problem of integration rather than vocabulary: work on main ideas, text structure and background knowledge rather than more glossing.

difficulties.pattern: 'I need to translate every sentence to understand it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Very slow reading, with written L1 glosses above most lines of the text.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that intensive translation is a familiar and sometimes useful study practice, then contrast it with tasks requiring overall meaning, and build fluency with easy texts where translation is unnecessary. Do not ban L1 use.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Why might a student who knows many reading strategies still fail to understand a journal article in English?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that strategies depend on recognising words and parsing sentences efficiently and that an unfamiliar topic also limits comprehension, and proposes different remedies for each.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions vocabulary or topic knowledge but treats difficulty as a single undifferentiated factor.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Attributes failure to not trying hard enough or to using strategies incorrectly.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, present the model concretely through activities rather than terminology. On pre-sessional courses, use it to explain the course's balance of vocabulary, fluency and strategy work. For postgraduates, a brief explicit treatment helps them understand why reading in a new discipline feels slow despite high general proficiency.
reviewNotes: The construct of a reader's situation model derives from van Dijk and Kintsch (1983) and Kintsch (1998); kintsch1998 is proposed because the closed bibliography contains only Kintsch and van Dijk (1978).

guidance.summary: Word recognition is the main bottleneck for reading rate and is built chiefly through exposure and practice with known words, not through strategy teaching; skilled reading speed reflects the efficiency of word identification (Rayner et al., 2016) and the quality of stored lexical knowledge (Perfetti, 2007). Koda (2005) shows that processing routines developed for the L1 writing system transfer to L2 reading, so learners whose L1 uses a non-alphabetic or non-Roman script may need more orthographic practice. Teach through high-volume easy reading, timed recognition activities and attention to word-family morphology.

activities.title: Timed word-family recognition
learnerActions: Scan rows of words and circle every form of a target family (analyse, analysis, analytical) against the clock
Repeat with new rows over several sessions and plot your time and accuracy
activities.intendedInsight: Recognition of known words speeds up with focused repetition, and morphology helps group forms quickly.
activities.rationale: Fluency-oriented practice with known material builds automaticity (Nation, 2009); attention to derivational morphology supports recognition of academic word families.

activities.title: Easy-text repeated reading
learnerActions: Read a 300-word passage with almost no unknown words and record your time
Reread it twice more, timing each reading
Read a new passage using the same vocabulary and compare the time
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated encounters with known words make recognition faster, and some of the gain carries over to new texts with familiar vocabulary.
activities.rationale: Repeated reading is a widely recommended fluency activity (Grabe, 2009); including a new passage tests transfer rather than memory of one text.

difficulties.pattern: Misreads visually similar words such as casual/causal or adopt/adapt, especially when reading quickly.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehension errors traceable to a single misrecognised word; misreadings during reading aloud.
difficulties.response: Explain that word-processing routines developed for the L1 writing system carry over into English (Koda, 2005), and give targeted contrastive practice with such pairs in context. Do not treat the errors as carelessness.

difficulties.pattern: 'I know this word' — but recognising it still takes noticeable effort.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate but slow completion of timed tasks; fatigue and declining comprehension in long texts.
difficulties.response: Provide large amounts of easy reading and timed practice with known words. Do not respond only by teaching more new vocabulary: knowing a word and recognising it automatically are different stages.

difficulties.pattern: Gaps in high-frequency vocabulary disrupt reading of otherwise accessible texts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Low scores on a vocabulary size test at the 2,000–3,000 family levels; frequent stops at common words such as whereas, despite or tend.
difficulties.response: Return to systematic high-frequency vocabulary learning supported by graded reading; academic word lists add little while the high-frequency base is incomplete.

diagnostic.task: A two-minute sentence-verification task built from high-frequency vocabulary, followed by a short vocabulary-size check.
diagnostic.strongResponse: High accuracy and a completion rate comparable to proficient peers.
diagnostic.partialResponse: High accuracy but noticeably slow completion, indicating that known words are not yet recognised automatically.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Low accuracy on items built from common words, indicating gaps in the high-frequency vocabulary base.

guidance.contextNotes: Most relevant at foundation and pre-sessional level, where gains in automaticity pay off most. In-sessional undergraduates who read slowly may be better served by self-access fluency programmes than by class time. Postgraduates rarely need explicit work here except with unfamiliar technical vocabulary.

guidance.summary: Treat fluency as rate plus comprehension and build it through a dedicated fluency strand of timed reading of easy texts, repeated reading and extensive reading (Nation, 2009; Grabe, 2009). Rayner et al. (2016) review eye-movement and comprehension research and conclude that speed-reading techniques claiming very high rates trade away comprehension, and that the sustainable route to faster reading is practice and a larger vocabulary. Set targets from each learner's own baseline, keep comprehension checks low-stakes, and use L1 adult norms (Brysbaert, 2019) only as a rough orientation.

activities.title: Timed reading programme
learnerActions: Read a short passage written well within your vocabulary level and note your time
Answer a few comprehension questions without looking back
Record words per minute and your score on a progress chart
Repeat two or three times a week across the course
activities.intendedInsight: Rate can increase on easy text without loss of comprehension, and progress becomes visible.
activities.rationale: Speed-reading courses built on easy, controlled-vocabulary texts are a recommended fluency activity (Nation, 2009); the comprehension check prevents rate gains being bought by skimming.

activities.title: Speed-reading claims check
learnerActions: Read a short advertisement or blog post promising very high reading speeds
Read a teacher-prepared summary of what eye-movement research says about word identification and comprehension
In pairs, explain why the promised rates are implausible and what realistic improvement looks like
activities.intendedInsight: Faster reading comes from more efficient word recognition and practice; very fast 'reading' is skimming with reduced comprehension.
activities.rationale: Confronts a persistent myth with the evidence reviewed by Rayner et al. (2016) and redirects motivation towards practice that works.

difficulties.pattern: 'Good readers read every text at the same high speed.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners rush dense methodological or theoretical sections and then misreport them.
difficulties.response: Teach rate flexibility: faster on familiar or low-priority text, slower on dense argument. Do not set a single words-per-minute target for all text types.

difficulties.pattern: Rereads lines habitually, even when nothing was misunderstood, for fear of missing something.
difficulties.revealedBy: Slow rates on easy texts; learners report anxiety about missing details.
difficulties.response: Use easy texts and timed practice to build trust in first-pass comprehension, and normalise purposeful looking back at genuinely difficult sentences. Do not forbid regressions; some are functional.

difficulties.pattern: Rate stays low because recognising common words is still effortful.
difficulties.revealedBy: Slow rates even on graded texts, combined with good untimed comprehension.
difficulties.response: Return to automatic word-recognition work and extensive reading before timed practice with academic passages.

diagnostic.task: Timed silent reading of a 400–500-word easy text followed by five comprehension questions answered without looking back.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A rate approaching the learner's target for easy text with most questions answered correctly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Good comprehension at a markedly slow rate, or a fast rate with weak comprehension.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Slow rate and weak comprehension even on easy text, suggesting vocabulary or word-recognition gaps rather than a fluency problem.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional programmes can timetable a regular fluency strand. In-sessional learners benefit from self-access timed reading with progress charts. For postgraduates the focus shifts to rate flexibility across specialist text types and to realistic planning; very high rates are not a goal. Adapt timed reading for learners with dyslexia, visual impairment or other access needs, for example with text-to-speech or untimed versions.
reviewNotes: Published rate norms come mainly from L1 English adult readers; L2 academic readers will usually read more slowly, and no norm should be used as a pass mark.

guidance.summary: Day and Bamford (1998) set out widely adopted principles: easy material, wide choice, learner selection, large quantity, reading for meaning and pleasure, and the teacher as role model. A meta-analysis indicates a positive overall effect of extensive reading on reading proficiency, with effects varying by learner and programme characteristics (Jeon & Day, 2016), and Beglar et al. (2012) found reading-rate gains among university EFL learners reading for pleasure, larger for those who read more simplified text. In EAP, extensive reading can be bridged towards academic content through popular science and narrow reading on one topic, but ease must be preserved.

activities.title: Self-selected reading with a level check
learnerActions: Choose a graded reader or accessible non-fiction text from a class or online library
Read one page and count unknown words; move down a level if there are more than a few
Read for 20–30 minutes a day and log pages, time and a one-line response
activities.intendedInsight: Volume of reading at an easy level is what builds fluency and confidence.
activities.rationale: Applies core extensive reading principles and the high-coverage condition for unassisted reading (Day & Bamford, 1998; Nation, 2009).

activities.title: Narrow reading bridge
learnerActions: Choose a topic linked to your future discipline
Read several accessible texts on it in sequence, such as popular-science articles, magazine features and introductory chapters
Note which terms and ideas become easier with each new text
activities.intendedInsight: Reading many texts on one topic recycles vocabulary and knowledge, so later texts become easier.
activities.rationale: Narrow reading increases repeated encounters with topic vocabulary, supporting incidental learning (Nation, 2013), while extending extensive reading towards academic content.

difficulties.pattern: 'Easy books are for children; I should be reading academic texts.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners choose texts far above their level and soon abandon reading.
difficulties.response: Explain that fluency is built only on text that is easy for the reader and that graded readers for adults exist. Offer graded non-fiction and accessible academic topics rather than insisting on fiction.

difficulties.pattern: Turns extensive reading into intensive study, looking up every unknown word.
difficulties.revealedBy: Low page counts in logs; dictionary-annotated pages.
difficulties.response: Show why extensive reading needs very high coverage, set a minimal-dictionary rule and move to an easier level. Do not attach comprehension tests to every book.

difficulties.pattern: Reading lapses after the first few weeks.
difficulties.revealedBy: Irregular entries in reading logs and no change in rate.
difficulties.response: Build reading time into class, use brief book talks and peer recommendations, and treat the log as a record rather than a test.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to summarise the last few pages of their current extensive reading text and note unknown words on one page.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Few or no unknown words and an easy, accurate summary.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Several unknown words but an adequate summary; the level could be lowered.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Many unknown words and no clear summary; the text is not functioning as extensive reading.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes can run sustained extensive reading throughout the year. Short pre-sessionals are unlikely to show measurable gains on their own, so extensive reading should be framed as a habit to continue into the degree. In-sessional learners can bridge to popular-science and disciplinary magazines; postgraduates may use narrow reading in their field for fluency and background knowledge.
reviewNotes: Evidence for measurable extensive reading gains on short (6–12-week) pre-sessional courses is limited; most positive findings come from longer programmes.

guidance.summary: Grabe and Stoller (2011) distinguish reading purposes such as searching for information, reading quickly for gist, reading to learn, reading to integrate information, reading to write and reading to critique, each implying different processing. Teach purpose-setting as the first decision in any reading task and require learners to articulate it. Metacognitive inventories such as MARSI include setting a purpose as a global strategy (Mokhtari & Reichard, 2002), but reported awareness does not guarantee use, so observe what learners actually do.

activities.title: One text, three purposes
learnerActions: Receive one article with three different task cards (find a statistic, summarise the argument, evaluate the method)
Plan how you would read for each card: which sections, what speed, what notes
Carry out one plan and compare with peers who had different cards
activities.intendedInsight: How you should read depends on why you are reading; one text can legitimately be read in several ways.
activities.rationale: Operationalises the purpose categories in Grabe and Stoller (2011) and shows that selective reading can be principled.

activities.title: Purpose statements with a stopping rule
learnerActions: Before each assigned reading, write a one-sentence purpose and a 'done when…' criterion
After reading, check whether the criterion was met and what you would do differently
activities.intendedInsight: An explicit purpose gives a stopping rule and makes reading more efficient.
activities.rationale: Goal-setting and self-evaluation are core phases of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman, 2002), and purpose-setting is a global reading strategy (Mokhtari & Reichard, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: 'I must read every word from beginning to end or I am not really reading.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Uniformly slow reading of all texts regardless of task; weekly reading left unfinished.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that careful reading is often right, then show tasks where lecturers expect partial reading. Do not replace careful reading with skimming across the board.

difficulties.pattern: States a vague purpose such as 'to understand the text'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Purpose statements that could apply to any text.
difficulties.response: Model task-specific purpose statements tied to an assignment or seminar question and give feedback on their specificity.

diagnostic.task: Give two different tasks for one text and ask the learner to describe their reading plan for each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Two clearly different plans tied to the tasks, covering sections, speed and notes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some differentiation, such as speed, but the same sequence and scope for both.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The same plan for both tasks.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need explicit modelling with short texts. Pre-sessional courses should tie purpose to assessed tasks. In-sessional undergraduates and postgraduates benefit most from linking purpose to seminar preparation and assignment questions, since over-careful reading of everything is a common cause of overload.

guidance.summary: Academic written English compresses meaning into noun phrases with extensive pre- and post-modification and nominalisation, leaving logical relations implicit (Biber & Gray, 2010, 2016). Readers used to clausal, conversational English often take a noun inside a modifier for the subject, or a participle for the main verb. Teach parsing explicitly with authentic sentences from learners' disciplines, using guided detailed reading that moves from the main clause outwards (Rose & Martin, 2012), and fade support as learners internalise the routine.

activities.title: Find the core
learnerActions: Take a 40-word sentence from a textbook or article in your field
Bracket prepositional phrases and relative or participle clauses
Underline the main verb and the head noun of its subject
Write the core proposition in under ten words, then add back one qualification at a time
activities.intendedInsight: Long academic sentences have a short core; most of the length is modification.
activities.rationale: Makes visible the phrasal compression that distinguishes academic writing from conversation (Biber & Gray, 2010).

activities.title: Guided detailed reading
learnerActions: Listen as the teacher paraphrases a sentence's meaning in everyday language
Locate, prompted by teacher cues, the wording that carries each part of that meaning
Highlight the nominalisations and say what process each stands for
activities.intendedInsight: Nominalised wording can be unpacked into who did what to whom.
activities.rationale: Adapted from the detailed-reading cycle of Reading to Learn pedagogy, which supports access to dense written text through guided sentence-level work (Rose & Martin, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Takes the first noun of a premodified noun phrase as its head (reading 'student writing assessment criteria' as being about students).
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that misidentify what a noun phrase refers to; wrong answers to questions about the subject of a sentence.
difficulties.response: Teach that the head of an English noun phrase is normally its final noun and that preceding nouns classify it; practise rewriting premodifier strings as postmodified phrases (criteria for assessing student writing).

difficulties.pattern: Takes the noun nearest the verb as its subject, or reads a past participle as the main verb (the method used in the study showed…).
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries attributing actions to the wrong entity; garden-path misreadings of reduced relative clauses.
difficulties.response: Locate the head noun before any postmodifying phrase or clause, use subject–verb agreement as a check, and reconstruct reduced relatives in full (that was used) while looking for a second finite verb.

difficulties.pattern: Can gloss every word of a nominalisation but cannot say what process it refers to.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correct translation of 'the reduction of' with no idea of what was reduced, by whom or why.
difficulties.response: Unpack nominalisations into clauses and repack them, using examples from the learners' disciplines.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to reduce a 45-word sentence from an article in their field to its core claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct subject, verb and claim, with the key qualification noted.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct topic but the wrong relation, or the claim without its qualification.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A noun from a modifying phrase is treated as the subject, producing a different claim.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from intensive guided practice with textbook sentences. Pre-sessional and in-sessional work should use texts from target disciplines, since compression patterns vary (heavy premodification in science, long nominal groups in social theory). Postgraduates may need this mainly for dense theoretical, legal or policy prose.

guidance.summary: Schema-theoretic research established that readers' content knowledge and knowledge of text organisation strongly affect L2 comprehension (Carrell & Eisterhold, 1983; Carrell, 1985). Grabe (2009) treats background knowledge as one of several interacting resources that becomes more important as texts become more specialised. Teach learners to activate what they know, to build knowledge deliberately through accessible sources before specialist texts, and to check that prior beliefs are not overriding what the text actually says.

activities.title: Know, expect, check
learnerActions: Before reading, list what you know and what you expect the text to say
Read and mark where the text confirmed, extended or contradicted your expectations
Revise your list and highlight any expectation you nearly attributed to the author
activities.intendedInsight: Prior knowledge helps prediction but can also distort recall of what the text said.
activities.rationale: Activating prior knowledge is a widely recommended pre-reading practice (Grabe, 2009); the final step trains readers to separate the text from their expectations.

activities.title: Build before you read
learnerActions: Before a specialist article, read an encyclopaedia entry, textbook section or review on the same topic
Note five key concepts and their relationships in a simple diagram
Read the article and add to the diagram
activities.intendedInsight: Reading an accessible overview first is an efficient, legitimate strategy, not a shortcut.
activities.rationale: Building content schemata reduces the knowledge load of specialist reading (Carrell & Eisterhold, 1983).

difficulties.pattern: 'If I don't understand, my English must be the problem.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Proficient learners report low confidence when reading in a new discipline.
difficulties.response: Help learners separate language problems from knowledge problems, and normalise background-building reading for anyone entering a new field.

difficulties.pattern: Reports what they believe about the topic rather than what the author argued.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries containing claims absent from the text.
difficulties.response: Require a line reference for each summary point and compare summaries with the text. Do not discourage the use of prior knowledge; teach checking it.

difficulties.pattern: Misreads texts that assume local institutional or national knowledge, such as references to a particular health system, legal precedent or policy.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehension failures concentrated on context-dependent references.
difficulties.response: Provide brief contextual glosses and teach learners to identify and look up assumed knowledge, treating this as a feature of texts written for a local readership rather than as a learner deficit.

diagnostic.task: Give a short specialist text on a topic unfamiliar to the learner with an accessible overview available, and observe whether and how they use it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses the overview strategically and can explain how it helped with the specialist text.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reads the overview but does not connect it to the specialist text.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Ignores the available background material and struggles with the specialist text.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners often meet unfamiliar subject content in content modules taught alongside EAP; integrate background-building with those modules. On pre-sessionals, choose texts linked to learners' future fields where possible. PGT students changing discipline and PGR students reading across fields benefit most from explicit background-building routines.
reviewNotes: Schema theory has been criticised as underspecified as a cognitive model; it is used here as a practical framing, with Grabe (2009) and construction–integration models as the more current theoretical basis.

guidance.summary: University reading lists are often longer than students can read closely, and lecturers frequently expect selective reading; Leki's (2007) case studies show L2 undergraduates developing their own ways of coping with reading demands, not all of them productive. Teach triage as a purpose-driven judgement linked to module documents and assessments, combined with realistic time estimates from learners' own reading rates, within a plan–monitor–reflect cycle (Zimmerman, 2002). Be explicit that faster reading alone will not solve overload (Rayner et al., 2016).

activities.title: Reading-list triage
learnerActions: Take an authentic module reading list and the module's assessment brief
Label each item essential, useful or optional and justify the label
Estimate how long each essential item will take using your measured reading rate
Compare your plan with a lecturer's or a more experienced student's view
activities.intendedInsight: Not everything on a list is meant to be read in full; priorities follow from teaching and assessment.
activities.rationale: Makes tacit expectations about reading lists explicit and links reading choices to purpose (Grabe & Stoller, 2011).

activities.title: Plan, monitor, review
learnerActions: Draft a weekly reading schedule
Record the time actually spent and what was read
At the end of the week, compare plan and reality and adjust the next plan
activities.intendedInsight: Reading plans become realistic when they are tested against one's actual pace.
activities.rationale: Applies the forethought, performance and self-reflection phases of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: 'I'm behind because I read too slowly, so I'll learn speed reading.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Interest in speed-reading apps; plans that assume unrealistic rates.
difficulties.response: Explain the evidence on speed reading and shift the solution to prioritising and planned partial reading. Do not promise rate gains that would remove the need to select.

difficulties.pattern: Reads optional items closely and skips essential ones.
difficulties.revealedBy: Seminar contributions based on peripheral reading; assignments missing core sources.
difficulties.response: Teach reading-list conventions (core, essential, further) and how they relate to assessment, and require a purpose statement for each item read.

difficulties.pattern: Stops reading altogether after falling behind.
difficulties.revealedBy: A sudden drop in preparation and avoidance of seminars.
difficulties.response: Help the learner reprioritise to the minimum viable reading for the next session, and refer to support services where workload is affecting wellbeing.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they decided what to read for last week's seminar and how long it took.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes clear priorities linked to the seminar question and accurate use of time.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Has priorities but unrealistic time estimates.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Read in list order or not at all, with no basis for choice.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need guidance on what reading lists are and how they relate to modules. Pre-sessional courses can simulate realistic loads. In-sessional undergraduates and PGT students face the sharpest overload, PGT timelines being especially compressed. PGR researchers need longer-term strategies for sustaining reading of a literature alongside writing.
reviewNotes: Expectations about how much of a reading list students should read vary by discipline and lecturer; teachers should gather local evidence rather than generalise.

guidance.summary: A meta-analysis found a modest comprehension advantage for paper over screen for expository texts, especially under time constraints (Delgado et al., 2018), which suggests that the risk lies in faster, shallower processing habits rather than in technology itself. Teach learners to match medium to purpose, to use PDF tools for purposeful annotation rather than mass highlighting, which is a low-utility technique (Dunlosky et al., 2013), and to check unfamiliar web sources by reading laterally as professional fact-checkers do (Wineburg & McGrew, 2019). Do not present screen reading as inherently inferior: most university reading is now digital.

activities.title: Screen versus paper reflection
learnerActions: Read one short article on screen and a comparable one on paper, each with the same type of question
Write an unaided three-sentence summary after each
Compare the summaries and reflect on how you read in each medium (speed, distraction, annotation)
activities.intendedInsight: Felt understanding can exceed actual understanding, particularly after fast screen reading.
activities.rationale: Invites learners to test against their own experience the screen disadvantage for expository text under time pressure reported by Delgado et al. (2018).

activities.title: Purposeful PDF annotation
learnerActions: Set a reading purpose for a PDF article
Use at most two highlight colours with defined meanings and add margin comments in your own words
List your comments and check whether they answer your purpose
activities.intendedInsight: Annotation helps when it records your thinking, not when it marks most of the page.
activities.rationale: Highlighting alone has low utility for learning (Dunlosky et al., 2013); writing comments requires generative processing.

difficulties.pattern: Highlights large parts of a PDF and treats the text as read.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavily coloured PDFs combined with weak recall.
difficulties.response: Limit highlighting and require margin comments in the learner's own words. Do not ban highlighting.

difficulties.pattern: Follows hyperlinks or switches tabs and loses the thread of the main text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fragmented notes and long reading sessions with little progress.
difficulties.response: Agree a link policy (note links to follow later) and use focus modes, downloaded copies or print for close reading.

difficulties.pattern: 'I read it, so I understood it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident self-ratings alongside weak unaided summaries after screen reading.
difficulties.response: Build closed-file summaries into screen-reading tasks so that learners calibrate their judgement.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show their annotated PDF of a recent reading and to state, without looking, the author's main argument.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Sparse, purposeful annotations and an accurate account of the argument.
diagnostic.partialResponse: An accurate account, but annotations unrelated to any purpose.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Extensive highlighting and a vague or inaccurate account.

guidance.contextNotes: Learners at every stage read mainly on screen. Foundation and pre-sessional learners may need basic PDF and e-book skills; in-sessional learners benefit from discussing medium choice for heavy reading; postgraduate researchers need workflows that link PDF annotation to reference managers and notes.
reviewNotes: Screen-reading research changes quickly with technology and habits; the proposed meta-analysis (delgado2018) should be checked against more recent syntheses before publication.

guidance.summary: L2 reading draws on reading ability and conceptual knowledge developed in other languages (Koda, 2005; Cummins, 2008), and L2 readers report frequent use of support strategies such as translating (Sheorey & Mokhtari, 2001). A translanguaging perspective treats this as a resource rather than a deficit (García & Li Wei, 2014). The teaching task is to make L1 and machine-translation use strategic and checked: used to unblock rather than replace English reading, with verification of technical terms, hedges, negation and attribution, and with awareness of institutional rules.

activities.title: Machine-translation fidelity check
learnerActions: Machine-translate a short hedged paragraph from an article in your field into a language you know well
Compare the translation with the original, marking changes in certainty, negation, attribution and technical terms
Explain to a partner, in English, one change that would mislead a reader
activities.intendedInsight: Machine translation can help with gist but may alter the precise claims that academic reading depends on.
activities.rationale: Uses the learner's plurilingual repertoire as a resource (García & Li Wei, 2014) while building verification habits; translation quality varies by language pair and domain.

activities.title: Bilingual concept glossary
learnerActions: While reading a set of texts, record key disciplinary terms with the English definition from the text, an L1 equivalent and an example
Flag terms whose L1 equivalent has a different scope or connotation
Review the glossary before seminars
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalents across languages are often partial; noticing differences sharpens understanding in both languages.
activities.rationale: Builds on cross-linguistic transfer of conceptual knowledge (Cummins, 2008) while attending to mismatches.

difficulties.pattern: Translates the whole text before reading any of the English.
difficulties.revealedBy: Machine-translation output used as the reading text; inability to locate claims in the original.
difficulties.response: Set tasks that require line references to the English text and limit translation to flagged passages. Do not prohibit machine translation, which is unenforceable and removes a legitimate support.

difficulties.pattern: Accepts an L1 equivalent that does not match the disciplinary meaning, for example taking 'significant' in a statistical report to mean simply 'important'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misreadings of sub-technical terms in otherwise accurate summaries.
difficulties.response: Teach checking key terms against English glossaries and their use in context, and collect common false equivalents in the learners' languages.

difficulties.pattern: 'Using my own language is cheating or unacademic.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners hide L1 use or avoid useful L1 resources while understanding little.
difficulties.response: Discuss legitimate uses and institutional policy openly, distinguishing support for reading from submitting translated writing.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they handled the hardest part of their last reading and whether they used another language or a translation tool.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes selective, checked use of L1 or machine translation and knows the local rules.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses L1 or machine translation but does not check terms or hedges.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Either relies entirely on translation or avoids all L1 resources while understanding little.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit from explicit discussion and practice. In EMI and transnational settings, bilingual reading is often the norm and should be planned for. Postgraduate researchers may read substantial literature in other languages and need conventions for citing translated sources.
reviewNotes: Institutional policies on machine translation in reading and in submitted work differ and change frequently; local rules should be checked.

guidance.summary: Previewing is a global strategy in metacognitive reading inventories (Mokhtari & Reichard, 2002) and one of the most transferable strategies for academic reading, because it is quick and supports both relevance decisions and later careful reading (Grabe & Stoller, 2011). Teach it with authentic articles and chapters, always followed by a check of predictions against the text, and link it explicitly to purpose and source selection. As with all strategies, its benefit depends on learners being able to read the preview features themselves.

activities.title: Three-minute preview and check
learnerActions: Preview an article for three minutes using only the title, abstract, headings, figures and conclusion
Write predictions about its topic, type, main claim and structure
Read the article and score your predictions
activities.intendedInsight: A short, systematic preview gives a reliable framework, and checking predictions sharpens it.
activities.rationale: Prediction followed by verification turns previewing into active comprehension rather than a ritual (Grabe & Stoller, 2011).

activities.title: Relevance sort
learnerActions: Receive eight abstracts or first pages on a topic, together with an essay question
Preview each and sort them into read closely, read in part and not needed
Justify each decision to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Previewing is a decision tool for managing reading, not only a comprehension aid.
activities.rationale: Links previewing to source selection and the source-based writing demands of university study (Alexander et al., 2019).

difficulties.pattern: Treats previewing as wasted time and starts reading at the first line.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners cannot describe a text's structure until they have finished reading it.
difficulties.response: Demonstrate the time saved on a realistic task and make previewing a required first step in early tasks, always tied to a purpose. Do not assess previewing as a ritual detached from purpose.

difficulties.pattern: Relies on the abstract and treats it as the whole argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that reproduce the abstract's claims without the qualifications found in the discussion.
difficulties.response: Compare abstracts with discussion sections to show what abstracts leave out, such as limitations and qualifications.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to preview an unfamiliar article for three minutes and predict its main claim and structure.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate predictions drawing on several preview features.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate topic but a vague or inaccurate claim and structure.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Begins reading linearly, or makes predictions unrelated to the text.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners should practise with textbook chapters and short articles. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners apply previewing to source selection for assignments. Postgraduates use rapid previewing to screen large numbers of search results, often alongside reference management software.

guidance.summary: Skimming has a legitimate role in orientation and relevance decisions, but Rayner et al. (2016) show that it trades comprehension for speed: readers lose information in what they skip, so skimming serves gist and relevance decisions only when readers can identify the important parts. Materials shaped by test formats often over-teach skimming and scanning relative to careful reading for learning and argument, which Grabe (2009) and Grabe and Stoller (2011) identify as central academic reading purposes. Teach skimming as a bounded, purposeful technique and always pair it with decisions about which parts to read carefully.

activities.title: Skim, then decide
learnerActions: Skim an article in four minutes and write its gist and a section outline
Mark two sections you would need to read carefully for a given essay question
Read those sections and check whether the skim led you to the right places
activities.intendedInsight: Skimming is a route to careful reading of the right parts, not a substitute for it.
activities.rationale: Positions skimming within purposeful reading (Grabe & Stoller, 2011) while keeping its limits visible (Rayner et al., 2016).

activities.title: What did the skim miss?
learnerActions: Skim a text and answer gist and detail questions
Read the text carefully and answer the same questions
Compare your answers and list the kinds of information skimming lost
activities.intendedInsight: Skimming preserves structure and gist but loses qualifications, evidence and detail.
activities.rationale: Lets learners experience directly the speed–comprehension trade-off documented by Rayner et al. (2016).

difficulties.pattern: 'Skimming is how fast readers read everything.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners skim texts they are required to critique and then misrepresent the argument.
difficulties.response: Teach skimming as one reading mode chosen for a purpose. Do not set skimming as the default first and only reading of every text.

difficulties.pattern: Reads only the first sentence of each paragraph and assumes it states the paragraph's point.
difficulties.revealedBy: Gist statements that miss delayed or implicit main points.
difficulties.response: Show paragraphs whose point is delayed or implicit, and teach sampling of paragraph endings and evaluative language as well as openings.

difficulties.pattern: Matches question words to text words without reading for meaning, a habit formed in timed test preparation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fast, keyword-driven answers that fail when the text paraphrases the question.
difficulties.response: Use tasks with paraphrased questions and require justification of answers. Acknowledge that the habit was rational in the test context in which it was learned.

diagnostic.task: A four-minute skim of a 1,500-word article followed by a gist statement and a question about a qualification within one paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate gist and outline, and recognition that the qualification requires careful reading.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate gist, but an inaccurate answer about the qualification given with confidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: An inaccurate gist or a list of topics with no overall point.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners often arrive with test-driven skimming habits that need repositioning within purposeful reading. In-sessional learners use skimming mainly for relevance decisions and seminar preparation under time pressure; for postgraduates it is chiefly a literature-screening tool.
reviewNotes: The claim that skimming and scanning are over-taught relative to careful reading reflects practitioner analysis and reading researchers' emphasis on reading to learn; systematic evidence on the content of EAP materials is not in the closed bibliography.

guidance.summary: Scanning is a simple skill whose teaching value in EAP lies less in speed drills than in two habits: anticipating the form of the target, including paraphrases and word-family variants, and verifying the context once something is found. Grabe and Stoller (2011) treat searching for information as a distinct reading purpose. In digital documents, search functions do much of the mechanical work, so predicting search terms and checking context become the key skills.

activities.title: Paraphrase hunt
learnerActions: Receive questions whose key words are paraphrased in the text
Brainstorm possible wordings of each target before scanning
Scan, locate the information and read the surrounding sentence to confirm it
activities.intendedInsight: Scanning for meaning requires anticipating varied wordings and checking context.
activities.rationale: Counters the keyword-matching habit and connects scanning to vocabulary knowledge and purpose (Grabe & Stoller, 2011).

activities.title: Digital search versus print scan
learnerActions: Find specified information in a long PDF report using the search function
Find comparable information using a printed index or contents page
Discuss which search terms failed and why
activities.intendedInsight: Digital search is fast but only as good as the search terms; synonyms and word families matter.
activities.rationale: Reflects the digital format of most university reading and the dependence of locating information on lexical knowledge (Alexander et al., 2019).

difficulties.pattern: Stops at the first occurrence of a keyword without checking that it answers the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Wrong answers taken from sentences that mention the keyword in another context.
difficulties.response: Require learners to quote the full sentence and explain why it answers the question.

difficulties.pattern: Cannot find information worded differently from the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Success on verbatim items and failure on paraphrased ones.
difficulties.response: Teach prediction of synonyms and word-family variants before scanning, and connect the task to vocabulary development.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to find three paraphrased items in a long report.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates all three quickly and confirms each in context.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Locates only items worded as in the question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Reads linearly from the start, or gives keyword-matched wrong answers.

guidance.contextNotes: Mainly a foundation and pre-sessional focus, often already familiar from test preparation, so little class time is needed beyond the verification habit. At later stages scanning is embedded in work with databases, tables and reference lists.

guidance.summary: Main-idea identification corresponds to the macro-processes of comprehension models, in which readers delete, generalise and construct propositions to form a gist (Kintsch & van Dijk, 1978); Brown and Day (1983) found that the harder operations of generalising and inventing an implicit topic sentence develop late. Teach with authentic paragraphs in which main ideas are not always stated first, using sentence-function labelling and hierarchical outlining, and connect the skill explicitly to summarising and note-making.

activities.title: Sentence function labelling
learnerActions: Label each sentence of a paragraph as claim, explanation, example, evidence or qualification
Identify the claim that the other sentences support
Write the main idea in one sentence of your own
activities.intendedInsight: A main idea is identified by what the other sentences do in relation to it.
activities.rationale: Makes the functional hierarchy of propositions explicit, approximating the macro-operations described by Kintsch and van Dijk (1978).

activities.title: Constructing an implicit topic sentence
learnerActions: Read a paragraph that has no explicit topic sentence
Delete trivial and repeated information
Replace lists with a superordinate term and construct a topic sentence
Compare with peers and with how the writer uses the paragraph in the wider text
activities.intendedInsight: Sometimes the reader must construct the main idea rather than find it.
activities.rationale: Targets the generalisation and invention operations that Brown and Day (1983) found to be the latest to develop.

difficulties.pattern: 'The main idea is always the first sentence.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Main-idea answers copied from first sentences even when these are background or transitional.
difficulties.response: Present paragraphs with delayed and implicit main ideas and ask for evidence from the rest of the paragraph.

difficulties.pattern: Selects the most vivid example or statistic as the main idea.
difficulties.revealedBy: Main-idea statements that restate an example.
difficulties.response: Ask what the example is an example of, and practise generalising from specific to general.

difficulties.pattern: Copies a long sentence rather than stating the idea in their own words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Verbatim main-idea statements that include irrelevant modifiers.
difficulties.response: Require own-word statements of a fixed short length; if the learner cannot shorten the sentence, check whether they have parsed it. Treat copying here as a comprehension signal, not as an integrity issue.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph with an implicit main idea and a vivid opening example and ask for the main idea in one sentence of the learner's own.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate generalisation covering the whole paragraph.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A partly accurate statement that is too narrow or too broad.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the example or copies the first sentence.

guidance.contextNotes: Central at foundation and pre-sessional level, where it underpins summary and note-making. In-sessional work applies it to longer disciplinary texts and sections. Postgraduates usually manage paragraph-level main ideas but may need work at whole-article level, where the contribution can be stated subtly.

guidance.summary: Knowledge of how paragraphs are organised is part of the discourse-structure awareness that Grabe (2009) identifies as important for L2 comprehension, and Carrell's (1985) training study showed that explicit teaching of text structure improved ESL readers' recall. Teach paragraph patterns as probabilistic cues, using authentic paragraphs that include delayed and implicit points, and connect reading to learners' own paragraph writing. Avoid presenting the topic-sentence model taught for writing as a universal description of expert paragraphs.

activities.title: Paragraph reconstruction
learnerActions: Reorder the jumbled sentences of an academic paragraph
Identify the controlling sentence, the development pattern and any linking sentence
Explain which signals helped you
activities.intendedInsight: Paragraphs have an internal logic signalled by reference, connectors and general-to-specific movement.
activities.rationale: Reordering requires attention to coherence signals and structure, building the discourse awareness Grabe (2009) describes.

activities.title: Predict the paragraph
learnerActions: Read only the first sentence of several paragraphs
Predict each paragraph's development pattern and likely content
Read the paragraphs and evaluate your predictions
activities.intendedInsight: Opening sentences often set up expectations, but not always; checking predictions builds flexible use of structure.
activities.rationale: Prediction from structural cues engages readers with organisation, in line with structure-training approaches (Carrell, 1985).

difficulties.pattern: Expects every paragraph to follow the topic sentence–support–conclusion model taught for writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion with expert paragraphs that open with a counter-view, data or a question.
difficulties.response: Show the range of expert paragraph structures and distinguish a writing scaffold from a description of all paragraphs.

difficulties.pattern: Ignores connectors and treats each sentence as independent.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reordering completed by topic guesswork; contrastive sentences read as additive.
difficulties.response: Highlight connectors and the relations they express before reordering and prediction tasks.

diagnostic.task: A jumbled-paragraph reordering task that includes one paragraph with a delayed main point.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct order with signals explained and the delayed main point recognised.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct order explained only by topic, without reference to signals.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Incorrect order, with the first sentence assumed to be the main point.

guidance.contextNotes: Mainly a foundation and pre-sessional focus, linked to paragraph writing. In-sessional, it is better integrated into main-idea and text-organisation work with disciplinary texts than taught separately.

guidance.summary: Carrell (1985) found that explicitly teaching top-level rhetorical structures improved ESL readers' recall, and Hoey (1983, 2001) shows how patterns such as problem–solution and claim–counterclaim are signalled lexically and how readers use those signals to anticipate what comes next. Teach a small number of high-frequency patterns with graphic organisers, focus on signalling vocabulary, and move quickly to authentic disciplinary texts in which patterns are embedded and combined.

activities.title: Graphic organiser mapping
learnerActions: Identify the overall pattern of an article
Complete a graphic organiser for that pattern, for example situation–problem–response–evaluation
Underline the signalling words for each element
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the overall pattern makes long texts easier to follow and remember.
activities.rationale: Reproduces the core of Carrell's (1985) structure training, with signalling vocabulary drawn from Hoey's (1983) pattern analysis.

activities.title: Signal and predict
learnerActions: Read a text section by section, stopping at signals such as 'however, this approach' or 'a further problem'
Predict what the next section will do
Check and discuss your predictions
activities.intendedInsight: Writers signal their plans, and readers who notice the signals can anticipate.
activities.rationale: Draws on Hoey's (2001) account of reading as interaction in which the writer answers questions the reader is led to ask.

difficulties.pattern: Identifies a pattern from a single signal and forces the content to fit it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rigid organiser completion with content placed in the wrong slots.
difficulties.response: Use texts that combine patterns and require justification of each slot assignment from the text.

difficulties.pattern: Overlooks headings and frame markers.
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines that miss section-level structure.
difficulties.response: Begin outlining from headings and frame markers before reading for detail.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to outline a 700-word problem–solution text and name its signals.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate pattern mapping supported by signals.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct pattern identified, but elements incomplete or misplaced.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A linear list of content with no pattern.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses can teach patterns explicitly with accessible texts. In-sessional and PGT teaching should focus on how patterns appear in disciplinary genres, such as problem–solution in engineering and business reports and claim–counterclaim in humanities argument.

guidance.summary: Research articles follow conventional macrostructures and move patterns described in genre analysis (Swales, 1990, 2004), which readers can exploit to read non-linearly according to purpose. Wallace and Wray (2016) encourage postgraduates to read with a clear question and to be selective rather than reading everything from start to finish. Teach the functions of each section, practise purpose-driven routes through articles from learners' fields, and highlight disciplinary variation, including qualitative, theoretical and review articles that do not follow IMRaD.

activities.title: Article grid race
learnerActions: Receive an article from your field and a grid (question, design, sample or data, main finding, limitation)
Complete the grid in ten minutes, noting section and page for each entry
Compare the routes you took with peers
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing where information usually sits makes articles navigable without reading every word.
activities.rationale: Applies genre knowledge of research-article sections (Swales, 1990) to efficient reading.

activities.title: Purpose routes
learnerActions: For three purposes (relevance check, finding a method to adapt, evaluating a claim), plan a route through an article
Carry out one route and judge whether it was sufficient
Note where the article departed from IMRaD and how you adapted
activities.intendedInsight: Different purposes call for different routes through the same article.
activities.rationale: Combines purpose-driven reading with awareness of genre variation (Swales, 2004; Wallace & Wray, 2016).

difficulties.pattern: Reads every article from start to finish, including long methods sections, whatever the purpose.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very long reading times; notes dominated by methodological detail irrelevant to the task.
difficulties.response: Model expert reading routes and set timed, purpose-specific tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Assumes every article follows IMRaD.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion with theoretical, review or qualitative articles.
difficulties.response: Include varied article types and practise identifying structure from headings and introductions.

difficulties.pattern: Reads the abstract and discussion and reports findings without their conditions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Over-generalised reporting of findings in the learner's writing.
difficulties.response: Require one methodological condition (sample, setting, design) to accompany each finding the learner reports.

diagnostic.task: A ten-minute grid completion with an unfamiliar empirical article.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate grid with page references, reached by a non-linear route.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A mostly accurate grid reached by slow linear reading.
diagnostic.gapResponse: An inaccurate grid, or methods information not located.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses for postgraduates should introduce article navigation with articles from learners' fields. Undergraduates meet research articles increasingly in later years. PGT and PGR readers need it most; PGR researchers also benefit from discussing how experienced readers in their field read.
reviewNotes: Empirical studies of how expert readers navigate research articles are not represented in the closed bibliography; a suitable source could be added.

guidance.summary: Comprehension models treat inferencing as central: readers generate bridging inferences to connect propositions and knowledge-based inferences to build a coherent situation model (Kintsch, 1998; Grabe, 2009). Academic writing's phrasal compression leaves many logical relations implicit (Biber & Gray, 2010), increasing inferential demands on L2 readers. Teach inference as reasoning from textual evidence, distinguishing warranted inferences from speculation, and support it by building the background knowledge on which inferencing depends.

activities.title: Stated, inferable or unsupported?
learnerActions: Classify a set of statements about a passage as stated, validly inferable or unsupported
Underline the words that justify each decision
Discuss borderline cases with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Good inferences are anchored in the text; plausible ideas without textual support are not inferences from the text.
activities.rationale: Builds the distinction between text-based inference and free elaboration that comprehension research describes (Grabe, 2009).

activities.title: Making implicit relations explicit
learnerActions: Find a sentence in which a nominalised phrase hides a causal or contrastive relation
Rewrite it with an explicit connector or clause
Check whether your rewrite fits the rest of the text
activities.intendedInsight: Compressed academic phrasing often leaves the reader to infer how ideas are related.
activities.rationale: Targets the implicitness of phrasally compressed academic prose (Biber & Gray, 2010).
