difficulties.pattern: Adds personal knowledge or opinion as if the text had stated it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident answers that go beyond the text.
difficulties.response: Require textual justification for every inference and distinguish inference from personal response. Do not discourage elaboration; label it as such.

difficulties.pattern: Reads literally and misses implied evaluation or causation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that lose implied relations, or no answer to 'why does the writer mention this?'.
difficulties.response: Practise purpose questions about sentences and the unpacking of implicit relations.

difficulties.pattern: Builds an inference on a wrongly resolved pronoun or 'this'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inferences that rest on an incorrect antecedent.
difficulties.response: When an inference is wrong, check reference resolution first.

diagnostic.task: Three statements (stated, inferable, unsupported) about a short passage, with justification required.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct classification supported by textual evidence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct classification without evidence, or confusion between the inferable and the unsupported.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Unsupported statements treated as true.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need inference work with accessible texts and explicit modelling. In-sessional and PGT learners meet heavy inferential demands in dense disciplinary prose and in reading writers' implied positions, which connects this topic to stance and critical reading.

guidance.summary: Reference is a core cohesive resource (Halliday & Hasan, 1976), and academic writing makes heavy use of signalling nouns that encapsulate and evaluate stretches of preceding text (Flowerdew, 2003). For L2 readers, unresolved or wrongly resolved reference often goes unnoticed and undermines comprehension (Grabe, 2009), so teach it explicitly through reference-chain tasks, with particular attention to 'this/these + noun' and to reference to whole clauses and paragraphs.

activities.title: Reference chain arrows
learnerActions: Draw arrows from each pronoun, demonstrative and signalling noun in a paragraph to what it refers to
Mark items that refer to a whole clause or paragraph
Compare with a partner and resolve disagreements
activities.intendedInsight: Some references point to ideas, not single words.
activities.rationale: Makes cohesive ties visible (Halliday & Hasan, 1976).

activities.title: What is 'this'?
learnerActions: Find signalling nouns such as 'this problem' or 'these findings' in an article
Write a one-sentence summary of what each encapsulates
Check each summary against the preceding text
activities.intendedInsight: Signalling nouns summarise and label earlier text, steering the reader's interpretation.
activities.rationale: Based on Flowerdew's (2003) analysis of signalling nouns as text-organising and evaluative devices.

difficulties.pattern: Links 'it' or 'this' to the nearest noun.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misinterpretations where the referent is a clause or a more distant noun.
difficulties.response: Practise extended reference with explicit marking, testing candidate antecedents for agreement and sense.

difficulties.pattern: Treats synonyms and general nouns in a reference chain as different entities.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that count one study or concept as several.
difficulties.response: Trace lexical chains explicitly and discuss how writers vary wording for the same referent.

difficulties.pattern: Reads signalling nouns as neutral labels and misses their evaluation, for example treating 'this claim' as endorsement.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that present as established what the writer labelled a claim or assumption.
difficulties.response: Discuss how the choice of signalling noun can evaluate as well as refer, using contrasting examples.

diagnostic.task: Five numbered reference items in a 200-word passage; the learner states each referent.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All referents correct, including extended reference.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Pronouns correct, but encapsulating items resolved vaguely.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Several referents wrong, with a nearest-noun strategy evident.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit from explicit teaching. In-sessional work can focus on dense disciplinary prose and on links to the learners' own use of reference in writing.

guidance.summary: Academic texts present claims of varying certainty, supported by evidence and marked by hedges, boosters and attribution (Hyland, 1998). Kuhn (1991) found that many people do not reliably distinguish evidence from theory or explanation, which suggests that the distinction needs explicit teaching. Replace the fact/opinion binary with a richer set of categories and use hedging and attribution as linguistic cues to status.

activities.title: Status labelling
learnerActions: Label sentences in an academic paragraph as background, claim, evidence, evaluation or speculation
Circle the hedges, boosters and attribution that helped you decide
Discuss sentences whose labels are debatable
activities.intendedInsight: Academic statements differ in status, and language signals that status.
activities.rationale: Uses hedging research (Hyland, 1998) to link linguistic form to epistemic status.

activities.title: Evidence or claim?
learnerActions: Separate what a short argument claims from what it offers as evidence
Ask whether the evidence would convince a sceptical reader
Rewrite the claim so that its strength matches the evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Claims and evidence are different, and claims can be stronger or weaker than the evidence warrants.
activities.rationale: Targets the evidence–theory distinction that Kuhn (1991) found many reasoners blur.

difficulties.pattern: 'Facts are true and opinions are just personal.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Anything in a published source treated as fact; evaluative statements dismissed as 'just opinion'.
difficulties.response: Present academic knowledge as claims supported by evidence and open to revision. Do not simply swap the labels 'fact' and 'opinion' for new ones without changing the underlying view.

difficulties.pattern: Ignores hedges and reports a tentative finding as certain.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that drop 'may', 'suggests' or 'in this sample'.
difficulties.response: Teach hedges as meaning-bearing and check every summary for preserved certainty.

diagnostic.task: A four-sentence paragraph labelling task with cue words to be identified.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate labels, cues identified, and nuance on debatable items.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly accurate labels but reasoning in fact/opinion terms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: All published statements treated as fact.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need explicit work beyond the binary. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners should connect it to argument identification and to preserving claim strength in their own source use.
reviewNotes: What counts as established fact differs across disciplines (for example in physics and in history); examples should come from learners' fields where possible.

guidance.summary: Writers construct stance through hedges, boosters, attitude markers and self-mention (Hyland, 2005) and manage other voices through attribution and reporting verbs whose evaluative force signals endorsement or distance (Thompson & Ye, 1991; Hyland, 1999). Appraisal theory's engagement system describes how writers acknowledge, distance themselves from, counter or endorse other voices (Martin & White, 2005). Teach readers to track voices sentence by sentence and to read concessive structures carefully, since these are where misattribution most often occurs.

activities.title: Voice colouring
learnerActions: Colour each clause of a literature-review paragraph by voice: the writer, Source A, Source B
Circle reporting verbs and evaluative words
State the writer's position and the evidence for it
activities.intendedInsight: Academic texts are multi-voiced, and the writer's position emerges from how other voices are framed.
activities.rationale: Operationalises the distinction between averral and attribution and the evaluative role of reporting verbs (Hyland, 1999; Thompson & Ye, 1991).

activities.title: Decoding concession
learnerActions: Find sentences built on patterns such as 'Although X has argued…, …' or 'X is right that…, but…'
Identify which part the writer concedes and which part they assert
Paraphrase the writer's view accurately
activities.intendedInsight: In concessive structures, the writer's own position usually follows the concession.
activities.rationale: Draws on the engagement resources of concession and counter-expectation in Martin and White (2005).

difficulties.pattern: Attributes a cited view to the writer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries stating 'the author argues X' when the author reported X in order to reject it.
difficulties.response: Practise voice colouring and require the source of every idea to be identified in summaries.

difficulties.pattern: Reads all reporting verbs as neutral equivalents of 'says'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that turn 'claims' into 'shows'.
difficulties.response: Teach the evaluative range of reporting verbs with contrasting examples from the same text.

difficulties.pattern: 'Academic writers are neutral, so the writer has no opinion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report that a text expresses no position despite evaluative framing.
difficulties.response: Show how stance is expressed through lexical and grammatical choices in academic writing, and why tracking it matters for accurate source use.

diagnostic.task: A literature-review paragraph reporting three sources and critiquing one; ask whose view is endorsed and how the learner knows.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct attribution, with evidence from reporting verbs, concession and evaluation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct overall position, but one cited view misattributed.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cited views equated with the writer's own.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners need this to avoid misrepresenting sources in their writing. PGT and PGR readers need finer interpretation of stance in literature reviews and discussion sections, including disciplinary variation in how stance is signalled.

guidance.summary: Metacognitive monitoring is a hallmark of skilled reading (Flavell, 1979), and strategy inventories such as MARSI (Mokhtari & Reichard, 2002) and SORS (Sheorey & Mokhtari, 2001) indicate that more able readers report greater use of monitoring and problem-solving strategies. Reciprocal teaching combines predicting, questioning, clarifying and summarising with modelling and gradual handover (Palincsar & Brown, 1984). Teach monitoring through think-alouds and inconsistency-detection tasks, and be candid that self-report inventories measure awareness rather than use and that the effects of strategy instruction are variable (Plonsky, 2011) and are likely to depend on adequate language knowledge.

activities.title: Reciprocal teaching groups
learnerActions: In groups of four, take the roles of predictor, questioner, clarifier and summariser
Read a section, then perform your role aloud for the group
Rotate roles for the next section
activities.intendedInsight: Comprehension can be checked and repaired collaboratively, and the routine can then be internalised.
activities.rationale: Adapts reciprocal teaching (Palincsar & Brown, 1984), which was developed with younger L1 readers; use with adult L2 readers is an adaptation rather than a tested intervention.

activities.title: Spot the contradiction and calibrate
learnerActions: Read a text containing an inserted inconsistency and note anything that does not make sense
Rate your understanding from 1 to 5
Answer comprehension questions and compare your score with your rating
activities.intendedInsight: Feeling that you have understood is not the same as understanding, and monitoring can be trained.
activities.rationale: Targets the cognitive monitoring described by Flavell (1979) and builds calibration of self-judgement.

difficulties.pattern: Keeps reading after losing the thread, hoping it will become clear.
difficulties.revealedBy: Think-alouds with no pauses or repairs; vague summaries.
difficulties.response: Introduce stop-and-check points after each section with a quick self-question.

difficulties.pattern: Uses the same repair, usually rereading, for every problem.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated rereading of sentences whose difficulty lies in an unknown key word or missing background knowledge.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to match repairs to causes: a dictionary for a key unknown word, parsing for a tangled sentence, background reading for a missing concept.

difficulties.pattern: Overestimates their understanding of difficult texts.
difficulties.revealedBy: High self-ratings alongside low comprehension scores.
difficulties.response: Use calibration activities regularly. Do not rely on asking 'Do you understand?'.

diagnostic.task: A text with an inserted inconsistency, followed by a self-rating and four questions.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Detects the inconsistency, and the self-rating matches the score.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices confusion but cannot locate it; moderate calibration.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No detection and an overconfident rating.

guidance.contextNotes: Relevant at all stages. At foundation level, reciprocal teaching works well with short texts. On pre-sessional and in-sessional courses, embed monitoring in authentic reading tasks. Postgraduates more often need to detect subtle misunderstanding of specialist arguments than outright breakdown.
reviewNotes: Evidence for reciprocal teaching comes predominantly from school-age L1 readers; its use with adult L2 academic readers is a reasonable extrapolation, not an intervention tested in this context.

guidance.summary: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rate highlighting and underlining as low-utility study techniques, largely because they require little processing. Annotation adds value when readers summarise, question and connect in their own words, in line with Kiewra's (1985) depth-of-processing account of note-taking, although his review found the benefits of reviewing notes more consistent than the encoding benefits of taking them. Teach a small, purposeful annotation system linked to the reading task and to later note-making, and make the separation of author's and reader's ideas a routine part of it.

activities.title: Annotation audit
learnerActions: Compare two annotated copies of a text: one heavily highlighted, one with sparse highlights and margin notes
Use each copy to answer a question about the text without rereading
Decide which annotation was more useful and why
activities.intendedInsight: What matters is the thinking that annotations record, not how much of the page is marked.
activities.rationale: Shows learners the limits of highlighting as a study technique (Dunlosky et al., 2013).

activities.title: Margin summaries and questions
learnerActions: Write a three-to-six-word summary beside each paragraph
Add a question or response mark where you disagree or want evidence
Use the margin summaries to write a short summary of the text
activities.intendedInsight: Own-word annotations make later use of a text much easier.
activities.rationale: Generative processing during note-making supports encoding (Kiewra, 1985).

difficulties.pattern: Highlights most of the page.
difficulties.revealedBy: Annotated texts with most lines highlighted and no comments.
difficulties.response: Limit highlighting and require margin comments; return to distinguishing main claims from detail. Do not ban highlighting entirely.

difficulties.pattern: Annotations mix the reader's own ideas with the author's without distinguishing them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Later writing that blurs the boundary between source ideas and the writer's own.
difficulties.response: Use distinct symbols for the author's claims, views the author reports and the reader's responses, and link this explicitly to good source use.

difficulties.pattern: Annotates without a purpose, so the annotations do not help with the task.
difficulties.revealedBy: Annotations unrelated to the assignment question.
difficulties.response: Set the purpose first and annotate against it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to answer a question about a text using only their annotations.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Sufficient own-word annotations that allow an accurate answer.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Annotations partly useful, with reliance on highlighted source wording.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Annotations unusable without rereading the text.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need explicit annotation systems. In-sessional and PGT learners benefit from linking annotation to note-making and synthesis. Digital tools change the practicalities but not the principle.
reviewNotes: Research specifically on annotation in L2 academic reading is not represented in the closed bibliography; claims draw on general learning research.

guidance.summary: Textbooks construct disciplinary knowledge through dense technical vocabulary, taxonomies and nominalised explanation (Halliday & Martin, 1993; Schleppegrell, 2004), which makes them demanding for L2 readers despite their pedagogical apparatus. Teach learners to use that apparatus and to study actively: building glossaries and concept maps, explaining processes in their own words and self-testing with review questions, in line with the high utility of practice testing (Dunlosky et al., 2013; Roediger & Karpicke, 2006). On foundation programmes, coordinate with content teachers where possible.

activities.title: Chapter study cycle
learnerActions: Preview a chapter using its objectives, headings and summary
Read one section and build a glossary of the terms it defines
Close the book, answer the review questions, then check and note errors
activities.intendedInsight: Textbooks are designed to be studied actively, and self-testing reveals what was actually learned.
activities.rationale: Self-testing exploits the testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).

activities.title: Unpacking a technical definition
learnerActions: Find a technical definition or classification in a chapter
Identify the term, the class it belongs to and its distinguishing features
Restate it in everyday language and give an example of your own
activities.intendedInsight: Technical definitions compress knowledge into a predictable structure that can be unpacked.
activities.rationale: Addresses technicality and taxonomy as defining features of disciplinary language (Halliday & Martin, 1993).

difficulties.pattern: Reads the textbook once, like a story, and relies on rereading before tests.
difficulties.revealedBy: Good familiarity with the material but poor recall under test conditions.
difficulties.response: Teach study cycles built on retrieval practice. Do not recommend rereading or highlighting as the main study method.

difficulties.pattern: Copies definitions into a glossary without understanding them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Verbatim glossary entries and inability to give examples or non-examples.
difficulties.response: Unpack definitions and classifications explicitly and require an own example for each term.

diagnostic.task: Closed-book recall of three definitions and one application question after reading a section.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate definitions and a correct application.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Definitions recalled verbatim, but application weak.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Inaccurate definitions.

guidance.contextNotes: Most relevant on foundation programmes and in first-year undergraduate study, especially in sciences, business and economics. Pre-sessional courses can include a textbook unit for students going to textbook-heavy programmes. It is less relevant to postgraduate study.

guidance.summary: Graph comprehension depends on the reader's knowledge of the display type and of the content as well as on visual features, and novices tend to describe surface features rather than interpret relationships (Shah & Hoeffner, 2002). Friel et al. (2001) distinguish reading the data, reading between the data and reading beyond the data. Multimodal texts make meaning through the interplay of image and words (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006). Teach learners to move deliberately between prose and visuals and to check claims against the data.

activities.title: Text–visual cross-check
learnerActions: Read a results paragraph and its figure
List each claim the text makes about the figure
Check each claim against the figure and mark it accurate, overstated or omitted
activities.intendedInsight: Writers' descriptions of data can overstate or omit, and the visual is evidence to check.
activities.rationale: Develops interpretation beyond surface description (Shah & Hoeffner, 2002; Friel et al., 2001).

activities.title: Reading beyond the data
learnerActions: Identify one pattern in a visual that the text does not mention
Suggest an implication or question it raises
Compare your idea with the writer's discussion
activities.intendedInsight: Visuals often contain more than the text reports.
activities.rationale: Targets the 'reading beyond the data' level described by Friel et al. (2001).

difficulties.pattern: Skips figures and tables altogether.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries omitting key data; inability to answer questions about the data.
difficulties.response: Set tasks that can only be completed using the visuals, and teach readers to pause at each in-text reference to a figure.

difficulties.pattern: Describes visual features ('the blue line goes up') without interpreting the relationship shown.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accounts of figures that never name the variables or their relationship.
difficulties.response: Practise moving from description of marks to statements about variables and relationships.

difficulties.pattern: Misreads tables with several variables, units or notes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors with row and column headings, units or footnoted exclusions.
difficulties.response: Practise systematic table reading: title, headings, units, notes, then cells.

diagnostic.task: A results paragraph with one overstated claim about an accompanying graph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the overstatement and cites the relevant data.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Senses a mismatch but cannot specify it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts the text's claim without consulting the graph.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need basic integration practice. In-sessional and PGT learners in quantitative disciplines need close checking of claims against data; in qualitative and theoretical fields, conceptual models and framework diagrams are more common.

authorNotes: rds.skimming and rds.scanning as two separate topics risk reinforcing the test-driven over-emphasis on speeded strategies relative to careful reading; consider merging them into one 'selective reading' topic or reducing scanning's stage range further (I limited scanning to foundation and pre-sessional).

rds.fact-opinion-claim: the skeleton name preserves the school-level fact/opinion binary that the topic argues against. Suggest renaming to 'Distinguishing claims, evidence and their epistemic status' (I kept the skeleton name and reframed the description).

rds.research-article-navigation deliberately has no edge from res.imrad: the RES group already makes res.imrad depend on rds.research-article-navigation (reading before writing), and a reverse edge would create a cycle. IMRaD knowledge is taught within the navigation topic.

Prerequisite direction assumptions other groups should respect to avoid cycles: sta.averral-attribution, sta.concession-language, coh.text-patterns, coh.frame-markers, crt.questioning, crt.concept, crt.evidence-types, inf.source-evaluation, inf.citation-chaining, ntk.notes-from-reading, dig.machine-translation and lrn.metacognitive-knowledge are prerequisites of reading topics here and must not come to depend (directly or transitively) on the reading topics that use them.

Cycles avoided by deferring to other groups: PAR makes par.paragraph-unit depend on rds.main-ideas, so rds.paragraph-structure-reading no longer takes par.paragraph-unit as a prerequisite (reading paragraph structure precedes writing paragraphs). SRC makes src.reporting-verbs depend on rds.writer-stance, so rds.writer-stance no longer takes src.reporting-verbs (sta.concession-language used instead).

Cycles elsewhere in the current parts, not involving reading edges: crt.questioning <-> sem.questions-clarification (CRT and SEM each list the other); idn.diversity-as-resource -> acu.transition -> idn.intercultural-communication -> (idn.elf ->) idn.diversity-as-resource / acu.transition. rdc.critical-questions depends on crt.questioning, so the CRT/SEM cycle should be resolved by those groups.

Overlap: rdc.multiple-texts and rdc.literature-mapping (reading side) versus syn.synthesis-concept, syn.relating-sources, syn.thematic-grouping and syn.synthesis-matrix (writing side). Recommend the SYN topics take rdc.multiple-texts or rdc.literature-mapping as prerequisites rather than duplicating comparison-across-sources content.

Overlap: rdc.bias-perspective, inf.source-evaluation and crt.cognitive-biases. Suggested scope split: perspective and framing within a text (RDC); authority, currency and provenance of a source (INF); the reader's own biases (CRT).
Overlap: rdc.critical-questions versus crt.questioning. I treat crt.questioning as the general habit and rdc.critical-questions as its text-specific application.

Overlap: rds.annotation versus ntk.notes-from-reading. Recommend NTK treat annotation (in-text marking) as preceding note-making (separate notes), i.e. ntk.notes-from-reading may take rds.annotation or rds.main-ideas as a prerequisite.

Overlap: rdp.plurilingual-reading versus dig.machine-translation and idn.plurilingual-repertoire. Suggest dig.machine-translation focus on permitted uses and production, leaving receptive use of MT in reading to rdp.plurilingual-reading.

rdc.methods-critique is scoped as consumer-level critique; it overlaps with dhl.critical-appraisal (formal appraisal tools) and res.limitations (already linked by RES). Its EGAP classification is debatable; ESAP would also be defensible.

Gaps: (1) no topic on reading disciplinary genres beyond research articles and textbooks (reports, policy documents, case materials, grey literature) outside the Disciplinary Literacies strand; (2) no topic on reading-into-speaking (using readings in seminars) on the reading side, though sem.citing-in-speech partly covers it; (3) no topic on using AI summarisation tools as a reading aid and their risks, which falls between rdp.plurilingual-reading and gai.research-tools; (4) no topic on accessible reading formats and assistive technology for readers with dyslexia or visual impairment.
rdp.word-recognition is typed PROCEDURAL in the skeleton; it is arguably a linguistic/fluency competence rather than a procedure, but the type was kept.
